DECISION

On July 20, 2020, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
June 22, 2020 final order concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq. and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the following
reasons, the Commission MODIFIES in part the Agency’s final order.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this co mplaint, Complainant worked as a GS -2210-14
Information Technology (IT) Branch Chief at the Agency’s Region IV office in Atlanta,
Georgia. On April 4, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency
discriminated against him on the bases of disability (physical), age ( born in September 1955),
and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (identified as a witness for an EEOC hearing) when:

1 This case has been randomly assigned a p seudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2020004241

2
1. In early 2015, Complainant’s supervisor (S1) transferred one of
Complainant’s IT staff members without first providing notice;

2. On June 14, 2015, management detailed Com plainant’s IT Operations
Team Lead for 60 days without discussing the action with him, which had
a negative impact on Complainant’s daily activities with staff and day -to-
day operations;

3. On Se ptember 3 0, 2015, he was falsely accused of providing
unsatisfactory or untimely information regarding Critical Vulnerability
Progress Update reports;

4. On December 9, 2015, he was falsely accused of missing a deadline on an
IT Life Cycle assignment;

5. On December 15, 2015, he was purposely locked out of FedHR Navigator
and could neither review his third and fourth quarter evaluations nor
provide a response to the adverse comments made on his performance
appraisal;

6. On January 29, 2016, he was informed that:

a. He would receive an Unsati sfactory Performance rating for the 2015
reporting period;
b. He would be placed on a 60- day Performance Improvement Plan
(PIP);
c. His Within Grade Increase was being withheld; and
d. If he did not successfully complete the one -year probation period after
the PIP, he could be demoted, transferred, or terminated;

7. On February 4, 2016, he was placed on a PIP; and

8. On February 22, 2016, the Regi on Security Office Chief informed
Complainant that his Top- Secret Clearance was being down graded t o
Public Trust.

On October 3, 2016, 182 days after he filed his complaint , Complainant requested a hearing
before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ).
2 The EEOC’s Atlanta District Office received
Complainant’s hearing request on October 13, 2016.

2 The Agency did not notify Complainant until February 14, 2017, that, because the Agency had
not completed the investigation within 180 days of Complainant fili ng his complaint, he had the
right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ or to file a civil action.

2020004241

3
On December 3, 2016, a Supervisory AJ (AJ-1) issued an “Order Directing Agency to Produce
Electronic Complaint File”, which required the Agency to produce the complaint file within the
earlier of 15 days of receipt of the order or from receipt of Complainant’s hear ing request. The
order also notified the Agency that sanctions could be imposed if the Agency could not show
good cause for not providing the complete investigative file within 15 days or if the Agency
failed to adequately investigate the complaint in acco rdance with Equal Employment
Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110) (Aug. 5, 2015).

On February 28, 2017, Complainant filed a “ Motion for Default Judgment ” asserting that, more
than 300 days after he filed his compl aint, th e Agency had still not begun the investigatio n.
Complainant argued that the Agency’s failure to complete the investigation within 180 days
pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(e) compromised the integrity of the federal sector EEO process
and that a default judgment in Complainant’s favor was appropriate.

On April 12, 2017, the Agency responded to AJ -1’s December 3, 2016, order to produce the
investigative file . The Agency explained that, since November 2015, it had experienced an
interruption in conducting in vestigations because it did not have available contract investigators
who met the Agency’s security requirements . The Agency indicated that, despite utilizing a
competitive process to hire qualified investigators, it was still experiencing signific ant delays in
investigating EEO complaint s. According to the A gency, it had assigned Complainant’s
materials to an investigator and estimated that the report of investigation would be complete d by
May 22, 2017. Agency Response at 3.

On June 12, 2017, AJ -1 issued an “Order to Show Cause”. AJ-1 observed that the Agency had
failed to provide the investigative record within 15 days of receipt of the December 8, 2016 ,
order, and directed the Agency to show cause why sanctions should not be imposed within 10
days from the date of the order. The Agency did not file a response. On June 20, 2017, t he
Agency provided a copy of the investigative file to the EEOC and transmitted a copy of the
investigative file to Complainant on June 28, 2017.

On September 25, 2017, the Agency filed its opposition to Complainant’s m otion for default
judgment. The Agency argued that a default judgment was inappropriate because Complainant
could not establish a prima facie case of discrimination based on age, disability, or reprisal. The
Agency further argued that sanctions were not warranted because it had good cause for the delay
in completing the investigation : namely, the unavailability of investigators. In the Agency’s
view, its situation was distinguishable from other cases because the delay was attributable to “an
unanticipated security clearance issue that arose in 2015 in regard to FEMA’s contract
investigators”, rather than inadequate or untimely performance by Agency employees or contract
investigators. Agency’s Response at 27. Accordin g to the A gency, the delay did not prejudic e
Complainant nor undermine the integrity of the system. The 223-day delay in completing the
investigation, asserted the Agency, was not as significant as the delay in cases where sanctions
were imposed.

2020004241

4
On November 14, 2017, Complainant replied to the Agency’s response to the motion for default
judgment, noting that the Agency’s response was untimely and should not be considered.
Complainant argued that default judgment was appropriate because the Agency disreg arded its
obligation to investigate his complaint and had fa iled to timely respond to AJ -1’s orders.
According to Complainant, the Agency’s excuse did not absolve the Agency from its
responsibility to timely investigate complaints. Complainant also contended that th e
investigation was woefully inadequate, noting that the investigative file did not include his
affidavit, which he timely submitted to the EEO Investigator.

On March 5, 2019, the EEOC reassigned the case to a nother AJ (AJ-2). On June 28, 2019, AJ-2
issued an “Order on Complainant’s Motion for Default Judgment ” (Sanction Order), an “Order
Denying Agency Motion for Partial Dismissal ”, and an “Order to Produce Revised Report of
Investigation”.
3 In the Sanction Order , AJ-2 found that, although the Agency was required to
complete its investigation and provide the report of investigation to Complainant no later than
October 3, 2016, the Agency did not provide the investigative file to Complainant until June 28,
2017, 268 days after the deadline. AJ-2 a lso concluded that the report of investigation was
“deficient” because it included “hardly any documentary evidence” and because the affidavit
from S1 was “unsigned and therefore, unsworn.” Sanction Order at 2. AJ-2 stated that th e
unavailability o f invest igators did not amount to good cause and was an affront to the EEO
process that the Agency did not ensure it had the resources needed to timely complete
investigations.

AJ-2 found that, although the Agency’s actions warranted the imposition of sa nctions, default
judgment was not appropriate in this case. AJ -2 stated that default judgment was not warranted
after considering the following factors: (1) the extent and nature of the noncompliance and the
justification presented by the non- complying par ty; (2) t he prejudicial effect of the
noncompliance on the opposing party; (3) the consequences resulting from the delay in justice;
and (4) the effect on the integrity of the EEO pr ocess. However, AJ-2 did not explain why, after
consideration of these factors, default judgment was not warranted. Id.

Instead, AJ-2 ordered 12 hours of training, regarding the proper processing of EEO complaints,
for those Agency officials responsible for the inadequate number of investigators available to
investigate EEO complaints. In addition to identifying the responsible officials, the Agency was
required to file a statement explaining why it did not have enough EEO investigators to timely
complete investigations and what actions it has taken to address the problem. AJ -2 also found
that Complainant was prejudiced by the inadequacy of the investigation and ordered the Agency
to bear a portion of Complainant’s discovery costs. Specifically, AJ-2 ordered the Agency to pay
reasonable attorney’s fees for up to five hours preparing requests for production of documents
and reviewing the Agency’s responses to his requests for production.

3 In the Order to Produce Revised Report of Investigation, AJ -2 ordered the Agency to submit a
revised version of the report of investigation that had sequentially numbered pages.

2020004241

5
AJ-2 also ordered the Agency to pay for the costs of taking the depos ition of S1, including the
court reporter fee, the fee for one copy of the deposition transcript, and reasonable attorney’s
fees for up to 15 hours preparing for and taking the deposition.

On July 29, 2019, the Agency submitted statements from Office of Equal Rights (OER) Director
and the Civil Rights Program Manager in respons e to AJ-2’s “Order on Complainant’s Motion
for Default Judgment ”. The Agency indicated that the three employees (two former OER
Directors and the former Formal Complaints Unit Branch Chief) , who were responsible for the
Agency’s inadequate number of invest igators, no longer worked for the Agency. T he Agency
provided documentation showing that all three employees had retired or resigned , in 2017 or
earlier.

On October 15, 2019, the Agency filed a motion for summary judgment. Complainant responded
to the Agency’s m otion for summary judgment on October 30, 2019. In turn, the Agency
submitted a reply on November 6, 2019. The Agency’s motion and its reply relied on the
transcript of Complainant’s deposition, excerpts from the transcript of S1’s deposition, and other
documents that the Agency produced, for the first time, during discovery.

On May 8, 2020, AJ -2 issued a decision granting the Agency’s motion for summary judgment,
finding that there was no genuine issue of material fact regarding whether the Agen cy subjected
Complainant to discrimination based on age, disability, and/or reprisal. Regarding claims (1)
through (3), AJ -2 found that Complainant could not establish a prima facie case of reprisal
because S1 did not learn of Complainant’s EEO activity un til November 27, 2015, after the
incidents at issue . AJ -2 further found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory
reasons for its actions. AJ-2 determined that, because he asserted nothing more than unsupported
allegations and speculation that the actions were based on his age and/or disability, Complainant
was unable to establish pretext for age and/or disability discrimination. For claims (4) through
(8), AJ-2 noted that Complainant relied on the temporal proximity between when S1 learned he
was nam ed as a wi tness and the adverse actions, which AJ -2 reasoned was insufficient to
establish pretext for reprisal.

On May 8, 2020, AJ-2 also issued an “Order Regarding Filings to Address Appropriate Award of
Attorney’s Fees and Costs ”. Since the Agency officials responsible for the lack of investigators
were no longer Agency employees, AJ-2 declined to order the Agency to provide additional EEO
training. Complainant was ordered to submit a statement of attorney’s fees and costs , limited to
the discovery costs identified in the Sanction Order. Further, AJ-2 directed the parties to contact
each other by May 18, 2020, to discuss stipulating to the amount of attorney’s fees and costs.

On May 19, 2020, the parties filed a “ Joint Stipulation on Award of Attorney’s Fees and Costs”.
The next day, AJ-2 issued an “Order Awarding Attorney’s Fees and Costs as a Sanction Against
the Agency”, awarding Complainant the stipulated amount of $5,580.35 ($4,999.50 in attorney’s
fees; $580.85 in costs) . Additionally, AJ-2 issued an “Order Entering Judgm ent”, entering
judgment consistent with the May 8, 2020, decision and the Ma y 20, 2020, or der awarding
attorney’s fees and costs.

2020004241

6
On June 22, 2020, the Agency issued a final action implementing AJ-2’s decision.

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends that a default judgment was the only appropriate sanction in
light of the untimeliness of the investigation, the gross inadequacy of the completed investigative
file, as well as the Agency’s failure to abide by the AJ’s orders or timely respond to the motion
for default judgment. Complainant argues that he clearly established a prima facie case of
discrimination based on age and reprisal. T he Agency, asserts Complainant, should also be
responsible for attorney’s fees incurred for filing the motion for default judgment and during
discovery. According to Complainant, even if default judgment was found to be unwarranted,
other sanctions, such as drawing an adverse inference regarding S1’s testimony or barring the
Agency from filing a motion for summary judgment, should have been considered. Complainant
requests that the Commission vacate the AJ’s decision and issue a default judgment in his favor.

In response, the Agency contends that summary judgment was proper. According to the Agency,
default judgment would be inappropriate, and it was not an abuse of discretion for AJ -2 to tailor
the sanction as he did. The Agency requests that its final order be affirmed.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

In rendering this appellate decision, we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and factual conclusions,
and the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a)(stating that a
“decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on a de novo review…”);
see also EEO MD-110 at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (providing that an administrative judge’s
determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed
de novo).

Agency’s Failure to Timely Complete Investigation of EEO Complaint

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(e) provides that an Agency shall complete its
investigation within 180 days of the date of filing of an individual complaint. EEOC Regulation
29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f) states that an Agency shall provide the com plainant a co py of the
investigative file within 180 days of the date of filing an individual complaint. The procedures
contained in the Commission’s regulations are no more or no less than the necessary means to
eliminate unlawful employment discriminatio n in Federal employment. Mach v. Dep’t of Def. ,
EEOC Appeal No. 0120080658 (Nov. 30, 2010).

In this case, C omplainant filed his complaint on April 4, 2016. Complainant did not agree to
extend the investigative time period.
4

4 By written agreement, a complainant and the agency may voluntarily extend the time period for
no more than an additional 90 days. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(e).

2020004241

7
On October 3, 2016, when the A gency failed to complete the investigation within 180 days,
Complainant requested a hearing. On December 8, 2016, AJ-1 ordered the Agency to provide the
complete investigative file, within the earlier of 15 days from receipt of the order or from receipt
of Complainant’s hearing request. The Agency did not respond to the December 8, 2016, order
until April 12, 2017, and it never responded to the June 12, 2017, Order to Show Cause. The
Agency provided the report of investigation to the Commission on June 20, 2017, 442 days after
Complainant filed his complaint. It waited yet another week to transmit the report of
investigation to Complainant . As AJ -2 noted in the Sanctions Order, not only does the
unavailability of investigators to timely complete investigations EEO complaints not amount to
good cause, the Agency’s failure to ensure it had enough investigators is an affront to the
Commission’s regulations and the federal sector process. The Agency is ultimately responsible
for timely completion of investigatio ns of EEO com plaints, whether the delay is attributable to
contractors and Agency employees, or the failure of Agency officials to ensure the availability of
contractors. See Cox v. Soc . Sec. Admin., EEOC Appeal No. 0720050055 (Dec. 24, 2009);
Germain v. E nvt’l. Prot. Agency, EEOC Appeal No. 07A10048 (Dec. 23, 2002); Mitchell-
Wilcox v. Tenn. Valley Authority, EEOC Request No. 05920176 (Apr. 23, 1992). We agree with
AJ-2’s determination that the Agency failed to establish good cause for its f ailure to timely
complete the investigation, timely provide the investigative file to Complainant, and comply with
the AJ’s order.

Agency’s Failure to Develop an Impartial and Appropriate Factual Record

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(b ) requires, inter alia, that the agency d evelop an
impartial and appropriate factual record upon which to make findings on the claims raised in the
complaint. One purpose of an investigation is to gather facts upon which a reasonable fact finder
may draw conclusions as to whether a violation of the discrimination statutes has occurred. Id.;
EEO MD-110 at Chap. 6, § IV.B. A n investigation must include “a thorough review of the
circumstances under which the alleged discrimination occurred; the treatment of m embers of the
Complainant's group as compared with the treatment of similarly situated employees...and any
policies and/or practices that may constitute or appear to constitute discrimination, even though
they have not been expressly cited by the complaina nt.” Id. at Chap. 6 § IV.C. Also, an
investigator must identify and obtain “all relevant evidence from all sources regardless of how it
may affect the outcome.” Id. at Chap. 6 § VI.D.

Here, AJ-2 found that the report of investigation was deficient because it contained ha rdly any
documentary evidence and because the affidavit from S1 was unsigned and, therefore, unsworn.
Upon careful review of the record, we agree that the investigative file is severely deficient. The
investigation appears to have been severely rushed and perfunctory, as a result, the investigative
report does not even contain Complainant’s affidavit.

According to the report of investigation, the investigation was conducted between April 4, 2017,
through June 10, 2017, with the investigator sub mitting the investigative file to th e Agency on
the end date. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 3.

2020004241

8
In a June 9, 2017 memorandum to the record, the EEO Investigator noted that the matter was not
assigned to her until Tuesday, June 6, 2017, and the contractor responsible for the investigation
told her that the case was “due as soon as possible.” Id. at 92. The next day, June 7, 2017, the
EEO Investigator faxed and emailed the interrogatories to Complainant’s representative and also
spoke with his representative to express that a qui ck turnaround was needed . Id. The EEO
Investigator asked Complainant’s representative to return the complete d interrogatories as soon
as possible, no later than Wednesday, June 14, 2017. Id.

According to the EEO Investigator, a contractor (C1)
5 subsequently called and informed her that
the report of investigation was needed by June 9, 2017. Id. The record contains a series of June
7, 2017 emails between the EEO Inv estigator and Complainant’s representative. Id. at 93-94.
When Complainant’s representative pointed out that the EEO Investigator originally asked for
the interrogatories by Wednesday, June 14, 2017, and that her email moved the deadline up to
June 9, 2017, the EEO Investigator responded, “Yes, but [C1] has instructed me to finish the case
as soon as possibl e. Please do what you can and return as soon as possible. Next Wednesday
would be the very late st that I can accept the interr ogatory.” Id. at 93. The EEO Investigator
stated in the memorandum to the record, “On Friday, June 9, 2017, [C1] instructed invest igator
to use EEO Counselor report as statement for Complainant given the information was very
similar, if not the same, as wh at would appear in an interrogatory. The Report of Investigation
was written according to this instruction. The EEO Counselor report was used to provide the
statement of the Complainant.” Id. at 92. In another June 9, 2017, memorandum to the record,
the EE O Investigator stated that, “[d]ue to the urgency of completing this Report of
Investigation,” she interviewed S1 on Friday, June 9, 2017, which was his day off, and an
unsigned affidavit for S1 was being submitted. ROI at 96.

On June 13, 2017, Complainant submitted his completed affidavit to the EEO Investigator, but it
was not included in the ROI. See Reply to Agency’s Response to Motion for Default Judgment
at 4; Response to Motion for Summary Judgment at 4. By June 9, 2017, 431 days had already
passed since Complainant filed his EEO complaint, and 249 days had passed since the Agency’s
October 3, 2016 deadline to com plete the investigation.
6 It is nonsensical that the Agency could
not wait an additional four days to include C omplainant’s affidavit in the record , particularly
when Complainant re turned it in less than a week after receiving the questions and before the
original June 14, 2017, deadline. Complainant had already waited more than a year for the
Agency to investig ate his EEO complaint and obtain his statement. T he Agency’s failure to
thoroughly investigate his EEO complaint in accordance with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(b) and EEO
MD-110 not only resulted in a deficient investigative record, but also robbed him of the
opportunity to finally address his allegations of discrimination.

5 C1 is not identified, but the name of the contractor is “[C1’s last name] & Associates.” RO I at
92.
6 Because 180 days af ter April 4, 2016, landed on Saturday, October 1, 2016, the A gency’s
deadline to complete the investigation was the next business day, Monday, October 3, 2016. 29
C.F.R. § 1614.604(d).

2020004241

9
The Agency’s rush to complete its overdue investigation resulted in a near ly worthless
investigative record and is an affront to the federal sector EEO process.

Appropriate Sanction for Multiple Violations of 29 C.F.R. Part 1614

The Commission’s regulations afford broad authority to AJs for the conduct of hearings. See 29
C.F.R. § 1614.109 et seq.; EEO MD -110 at Chap. 7 § III.D. An AJ has inherent powers to
conduct a hearing and to issue a ppropriate sanctions, including a default judgment. See id.;
Matheny v. Dep’t of Justice, EEOC Request No. 05A30373 (Apr . 21, 2005); Rountree v. Dep't
of the Treasury, EEOC Appeal No. 07A00015 (July 13, 2001) . AJ-2 issued sanctions against the
Agency. AJ-2 determined that sanctions were warranted because the Agency failed to time ly
complete the investigation of Complainant’s EEO complaint and because the resulting
investigative record was deficient.

AJ-2 found that, although sanctions were warranted, default judgment was not appropriate in this
case. The C ommission has held repeatedly that sanctions must be tailored to each situation,
applying the least severe sanction necessary to respond to the party's failure to show good cause
for its actions, as well as to equitably remedy the opposing party. See Ward B. v. U.S. Postal
Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 2019001570 (May 12, 2020); Gray v. Dep't of Def., EEOC Appeal No.
07A50030 (March 1, 2007); Rountree , EEOC Appeal No. 07A00015; Hale v. Dep't of Justice ,
EEOC Appeal No. 01A03341 (Dec. 8, 2000).

The Commission's interest lies in deterring the underlying conduct of the non- complying party
and protecting its administrative proc ess from abuse by either party to ensure that agencies, as
well as complainants, ab ide by its regulations. See Royal v. Dep't of Vet . Aff., EEOC Request
No. 0520080052 (Sept. 25, 2009). The factors pertinent to “tailoring” a sanction, or determining
whether a sanction is, in fact, warranted, include the following: (1) the extent and nature of the
non-compliance, including the justifica tion presented by the non- complying party; (2) the
prejudicial effect of the non- compliance on the opposing party; (3) the consequences resulting
from the delay in justice, if any; and (4) the effect o n the integrity of the EEO process. Chere S.
v. Soc. Se c. Admin., EEOC Appeal No. 0720180012 (Nov. 30, 2018) ; see also Royal, EEOC
Request No. 0520080052; Gray, EEOC Appeal No. 07A50030; Vovsest v. Soc. Sec. Admin. ,
EEOC Appeal No. 01A35340 (Jan. 18, 2005).

The Agency argued in its response to Complainant’s motion for default judgment that its delay in
producing the ROI had no prejudicial effect on Complainant, that there were no consequences
resulting in a delay in justice, and that its actions did not undermine the integrity of the system.
However, we find that, not only did the Age ncy’s delay have a prejudicial effect on
Complainant, result in a delay in justice, and undermine the integrity of the system, the Agency’s
rushed investigation produced a shoddy, incomplete ROI, which compounded such harm.
Therefore, w e agree with AJ -2 that a sanction was warranted and consider the appropriate
sanction under the circumstances. AJ-2 ord ered training for the officials responsible for the
Agency not having enough investigators to timely complete EEO investigations and, because

2020004241

10
Complainant was prejudiced by the inadequacy of the investigation, ordered the Agency to bear
a portion of Complainant’s discovery costs.

The Agency not only failed to timely initiate or complete the investigation of the EEO complaint
but, as discussed, the Agency’s investigation was so rushed and deficient that it was an affront to
the federal sector EEO process. The Agency failed to show good cause for its delay. Moreover,
the Agency’s disingenuous attempt to establish good cause, by asserting it did not have enough
investigators to timely complete EEO investigations, r eflects serious disregard for the
Commission’s regulations. While the Agency contended that its delay was not as le ngthy as the
delay in other cases where default judgment was found to be app ropriate, we note that its delay
would have only been extended if it had actually fulfilled its responsibility to properly
investigate the EEO complaint. Moreover, the Commission ha s found that, “given the length of
time that the processing of a federal sector EEO complain t can take, any delays past the time
frames in the regulations can impact the outcome of Compl ainant’s cl aims.” Royal, EEOC
Request No. 0520080052.

The effect on t he integrity of the EEO process, the fourth factor, should not be underesti mated
when tailoring a sanction. Cox, EEOC Appeal No. 0720050055. “Protecting the integrity of the
29 C.F.R. Part 1614 process is central to the Commission's ability to carry out it s charge of
eradicating discrimination in the federal sector.” Id. (quoting Royal, EEOC Requ est No.
0520080052). An a gency that treats the time deadlines for production of an adequately
developed investigation as optional has a negative effect on the outc ome not only of the
immediate case, but also of any other cases under its ju risdiction. See id. Moreover, the Agency
repeatedly failed to reply to or comply with the orders of the EEOC AJ s. The Agency did not
timely comply with or respond to the December 8 , 2016, order to produce the complaint file and
did not respond to the June 12, 2017, order to show cause. Moreover, as discussed, the Agency’s
disingenuous arguments in its untimely resp onse to Complainant’s motion for default judgment
not only failed to establish good cause for the Agency ’s actions but also reflected serious
disregard for the federal sector EEO process. The Commission must ensure that all parties abide
by its regulations and orders.

Upon review, we find that, in addition to trai ning and bearing a portion of Complainant ’s
discovery request, the Agency should not be able to rely on evidence produced for the first time
during the discovery process in support of its motion for summary judgment or a motion to
dismiss. Additionally, the Agency cannot rely on affi davits in the investigative record or the
depositions in lieu of witnesse s who are unavailable to testify . This sanction will effectively
emphasize to the Agency the need to comply wi th Commission orders in a timely manner, as
well as ensure that future Agency investigations are properly developed for adjudica tion. See
Complainant v. Dep’t of the Air Fo rce, EEOC Appeal No. 0120132260 (July 17, 2015). This is
the leas t severe sanction that addresses the Agency ’s conduct and equitably remedies
Complainant.

2020004241

11
Based on the specific circumstances of this case, we also find it appropriate to order the Agency
to: (1) analyze its performance in conducting timely and adequate EEO investigations in
accordance with the Commission's regulations , during this Fiscal Year and the previous two
fiscal years, and to report its fin dings to the EEOC . In the event the Agency finds it is not in
compliance with the Commission's regulations on EEO investigations, the Agenc y is directed to
propose to the EEOC a corrective plan of action; and (2) provide training to its EEO personnel
who failed to comply with our regulations.

will effectively emp hasize to the Agency the need to comply with Commission regulations and
orders in a timely manner.

Discrimination Based on Disability, Age, and/or Reprisal
AJ-2 issued a summary judgment decision. The Commission's regulations allow an AJ to grant
summary judgment when he or she finds that there is no genuine issue of mater ial fact. 29
C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). An issue of fact is “genuine” if the evidence is such that a reasonable fact
finder could find in favor of the non -moving party. Celotex v. Cat rett, 477 U.S. 317, 322-23
(1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A fact is “material” if
it has the potential to affect the outcome of the case. We fi nd that the record is sufficiently
developed for summary disposition and that there are no genuine issues of material fact that
require a hearing.

To prevail in a disparate treatment claim, Complainant must satisfy th e three-part evidentiary
scheme fashioned by the Supreme Court in McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792
(1973). He must generally establish a prima facie case by demonstrating that he was subjected to
an adverse employment action under circumstances that would support an inference of
discrimination. Furnco Constr. Co. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567, 576 (1978). Proof of a prima facie
case will vary depending on the facts of the particular case. Mc Donnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at
802 n. 13. The burden then shifts to the A gency to artic ulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory
reason for its actions. Tex. Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). To
ultimately prevail, Complainant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the
Agency’s explanation is a pretext for discrimination. Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products,
Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000 ); St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502, 519 (1993); Burdine,
450 U.S. at 256; Holley, supra; Pavelka v. Dep’t of the Navy, EEOC Request No. 05950351
(Dec. 14, 1995).

Upon review, we agree with AJ -2 that Complainant fa iled to establish a prima fa cie case of
discrimination based on age and/or disability. Complainant offered nothing more than vague
speculation that he was subjected to discrimination based on disability. Moreover, because
Complainant s tated that his only limitations were that he could not run, crawl, or lif t heavy
objects more than 100 pounds, he has not established that he is an individual with a disability for
the purposes of the Rehabilitation Act. Complainant’s Interrogatory at 3.

7 Although AJ-2 did not order training be cause the three officials resp onsible for the lack of
available investigators were no longer employees of the Agency, we find that training is
nonetheless warranted for EEO personnel.

2020004241

12
In support of his age claims, Complainant state d that, in 2014, the new Acting Regi onal
Administrator (RA) said : “It’s now time for out with the old a nd in with the new” . See
Deposition of Complainant at 64-65. Complainant interpreted the remark as a plan to remove
and replace older personnel. The record reflects that the Acting RA made the remark in question
more than a year before t he alleged discri minatory actions at issue in this complaint, and the
Acting RA only worked in Region IV for a short period of time. See Deposition of Complainant
at 67, 85-86. According to Complainant, the new Deputy Administrator (DRA) appeared to be in
his mid-30s, and the new RA who subsequently replaced the Acting RA appeared to be in her
mid-40s. See Deposition of Complainant a t 65. Complainant alleged that his former supervisor
decided to retire immediately after his first performance evaluation with his new supervis or, the
DRA, rather than “putting up with what he was just put t hrough” during the performance
evaluation. See Deposition of Complainant at 65-66. We agr ee with AJ-2’s assessment, that the
Acting RA’s 2014 comment and Complainant’s former supervisor deciding to retire after his
performance evaluation with the new DRA are insufficient to establish an inference that
Complainant was subjected to age discrimination.

We further agree with AJ -2 that Complainant cannot establish a prima facie case of reprisal
regarding claims (1) through (3) . There is no evidence that Complainant engaged in protected
EEO activity before November 2015, or that S1 or other re sponsible management officials were
aware of such activity. However, we find that Complainant has established a prima facie case of
reprisal with respect to claims (4 ) through (8). Complainant stated that he engaged in prot ected
activity when he was ident ified as a witness for an EEOC hearing.
8 An Agency attorney (A1)
emailed Complainant on November 27, 2015, notifying him that he was identified as a witness
for an upcoming EEOC hearing in Orlando, Florida. Agency Motion for Summary Judgment Ex.
3. Complainant stated that upon receiving the email, he informed S1 that he had been named as a
witness and asked how to pay for travel to Orlando for the hearing. Claims (4) th rough (8),
regarding instances of alleged discrimination between December 9, 2015, and February 22, 2016,
occurred in close temporal proximity to when management learned about Complainant’s
protected activity. Consequently, we find that Complainant has established a prima facie case of
reprisal.

The Agency argued that claim (8), the Agency’s decision to downgrade Complainant’s security
clearance, is not reviewable by the Commission pursuant to Dep’t of Navy v. Egan, 484 U.S. 518
(1988). We disagree . The C ommission does not have jurisdiction to review an agenc y’s
determination on the substance of a security clearance decision. Policy Guidance on the Use of
the National Security Exception Contained in § 703(g) of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of
1964, as Amended (Guidance), EEOC Notice No. N-915- 041 (May 1, 1989); Egan, 484 U.S. at
529. However, the legislative history of § 703(g) makes it clear that the Commission is not
precluded from determining whether the grant, denial, or revocation of a security cl earance is
conducted in a nondiscriminatory manner. See Guidance. Here, the record reflects that decision
to downgrade the security clearance required for Complainant’s IT Branch Chief position did not
involve the substance of a security clearance decision.

8 Complainant never ultimately testified at the hearing.

2020004241

13
The Chief of the Office of Security for Region IV s tated that the DRA ordered a review of
security clearances for the region and decided to downgrade security clearances for several
individuals, including Complainant , based on a national security clearance reass essment
announced by the Agency’s Deputy Admi nistrator. ROI at 45, 111- 12. In a n October 2, 2015,
memorandum regarding the security clearance reassessment, the Deputy Administrator
specifically stated, “The downgrade or cancelation of a security clearance as part of this review
is not the result of e mployees’ performance, trustworthiness, or conduct and has no effect on an
employee’s eligibility to hold a national security position or security clearance in the future.”
ROI at 116.

Further review of the record establishes that Complainant is alleging that the Agency’s process
was discriminatory, and he has not challenged the Agency’s judgment regarding his access to
sensitive information. Rather, Complainant contends that the DRA singled him out, noting that
Complainant was the only IT Branch Chief whose security clearance was downgraded .
Moreover, asserts Complainant, while downgrading his clearance, the DRA recommended Top
Secret clearances for two of Complainant’s subordinates, hampering his ability to supervise his
team. See Complainant’s Response to Motion for Summary Judgment at 11-12. Accordingly, we
determine that this claim does not involve the substance of a security clearance dec ision and that
Complainant has established a prima facie case of reprisal regarding the downgrade of his
security clearance.

Having determined that Compl ainant established a prima facie case of reprisal for claims (4)
through (8), we consider whether the Agency satisfied its burden of production. Although the
Agency's burden of production is not onerous , it must pro vide a specific, clear, legitimate, and
individualized explanation that provides an opportunity for Complainant to satisfy his ultimate
burden of proof of pretext. Lorenzo v. Dep’t of Def ., EEOC Reques t No. 05950931 (Nov. 6,
1997). We find that, without relying on the depositions and other evidence produced for the first
time during discovery, the Agency cannot meet its burden of providing le gitimate,
nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions.

S1’s unsigned investigative affidavit and the limited docum entary evidence in the investigative
record do not satisfy the Agency’s burden to provide legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for
accusing Complainant of missing the deadline as alleged in claim (4), fo r locking Complainant
out of FedHr Navigator as all eged in claim (5), or for the performance -related allegations in
claims (6) and (7). Regarding claim (8 ), although the investigative record contains a swor n
affidavit from the Chief of the Office of Security for Region IV and some documentary evidence,
the Agency has not identified a specific, clear , legitimate, and individualized explanation for
downgrading the security clearance for Complainant ’s position. We therefore find that
Complainant has established that he was subjected to discrimination based on reprisal as alleged
in claims (4) through (8) and remand the matter for further processing.

CONCLUSION

Therefore, after a careful review of the record, including Complainant's arguments on appeal, the
Agency's response, and arguments and evidence not specifically discussed in this decision, the
Commission REVERSES in part the Agency's final action and REMANDS the matter for further
action in accordance with this decision and the O RDER below. We AFFIRM in part the finding
of no discrimination on claims (1) through (3).

DECISION

On July 20, 2020, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
June 22, 2020 final order concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq. and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the following
reasons, the Commission MODIFIES in part the Agency’s final order.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this co mplaint, Complainant worked as a GS -2210-14
Information Technology (IT) Branch Chief at the Agency’s Region IV office in Atlanta,
Georgia. On April 4, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency
discriminated against him on the bases of disability (physical), age ( born in September 1955),
and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (identified as a witness for an EEOC hearing) when:

Complainant’s IT staff members without first providing notice;

2. On June 14, 2015, management detailed Com plainant’s IT Operations
Team Lead for 60 days without discussing the action with him, which had
a negative impact on Complainant’s daily activities with staff and day -to-
day operations;

3. On Se ptember 3 0, 2015, he was falsely accused of providing
unsatisfactory or untimely information regarding Critical Vulnerability
Progress Update reports;

4. On December 9, 2015, he was falsely accused of missing a deadline on an
IT Life Cycle assignment;

5. On December 15, 2015, he was purposely locked out of FedHR Navigator
and could neither review his third and fourth quarter evaluations nor
provide a response to the adverse comments made on his performance
appraisal;

6. On January 29, 2016, he was informed that:

a. He would receive an Unsati sfactory Performance rating for the 2015

b. He would be placed on a 60- day Performance Improvement Plan
(PIP);
c. His Within Grade Increase was being withheld; and
d. If he did not successfully complete the one -year probation period after
the PIP, he could be demoted, transferred, or terminated;

before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ).

order also notified the Agency that sanctions could be imposed if the Agency could not show

Complainant argued that the Agency’s failure to complete the investigation within 180 days

On April 12, 2017, the Agency responded to AJ -1’s December 3, 2016, order to produce the

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

In rendering this appellate decision, we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and factual conclusions,
and the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a)(stating that a
“decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on a de novo review…”);
see also EEO MD-110 at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (providing that an administrative judge’s
determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed

Agency’s Failure to Timely Complete Investigation of EEO Complaint

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(e) provides that an Agency shall complete its
investigation within 180 days of the date of filing of an individual complaint. EEOC Regulation
29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f) states that an Agency shall provide the com plainant a co py of the
investigative file within 180 days of the date of filing an individual complaint. The procedures
contained in the Commission’s regulations are no more or no less than the necessary means to
eliminate unlawful employment discriminatio n in Federal employment. Mach v. Dep’t of Def. ,
EEOC Appeal No. 0120080658 (Nov. 30, 2010).

Appropriate Sanction for Multiple Violations of 29 C.F.R. Part 1614

The Commission’s regulations afford broad authority to AJs for the conduct of hearings. See 29
C.F.R. § 1614.109 et seq.; EEO MD -110 at Chap. 7 § III.D. An AJ has inherent powers to
conduct a hearing and to issue a ppropriate sanctions, including a default judgment. See id.;
Matheny v. Dep’t of Justice, EEOC Request No. 05A30373 (Apr . 21, 2005); Rountree v. Dep't
of the Treasury, EEOC Appeal No. 07A00015 (July 13, 2001) . AJ-2 issued sanctions against the
Agency. AJ-2 determined that sanctions were warranted because the Agency failed to time ly
complete the investigation of Complainant’s EEO complaint and because the resulting
investigative record was deficient.

AJ-2 found that, although sanctions were warranted, default judgment was not appropriate in this
case. The C ommission has held repeatedly that sanctions must be tailored to each situation,
applying the least severe sanction necessary to respond to the party's failure to show good cause
for its actions, as well as to equitably remedy the opposing party. See Ward B. v. U.S. Postal
Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 2019001570 (May 12, 2020); Gray v. Dep't of Def., EEOC Appeal No.
07A50030 (March 1, 2007); Rountree , EEOC Appeal No. 07A00015; Hale v. Dep't of Justice ,
EEOC Appeal No. 01A03341 (Dec. 8, 2000).

The Commission's interest lies in deterring the underlying conduct of the non- complying party
and protecting its administrative proc ess from abuse by either party to ensure that agencies, as
well as complainants, ab ide by its regulations. See Royal v. Dep't of Vet . Aff., EEOC Request
No. 0520080052 (Sept. 25, 2009). The factors pertinent to “tailoring” a sanction, or determining
whether a sanction is, in fact, warranted, include the following: (1) the extent and nature of the
non-compliance, including the justifica tion presented by the non- complying party; (2) the
prejudicial effect of the non- compliance on the opposing party; (3) the consequences resulting
from the delay in justice, if any; and (4) the effect o n the integrity of the EEO process. Chere S.
v. Soc. Se c. Admin., EEOC Appeal No. 0720180012 (Nov. 30, 2018) ; see also Royal, EEOC
Request No. 0520080052; Gray, EEOC Appeal No. 07A50030; Vovsest v. Soc. Sec. Admin. ,
EEOC Appeal No. 01A35340 (Jan. 18, 2005).

The Agency argued in its response to Complainant’s motion for default judgment that its delay in
producing the ROI had no prejudicial effect on Complainant, that there were no consequences
resulting in a delay in justice, and that its actions did not undermine the integrity of the system.
However, we find that, not only did the Age ncy’s delay have a prejudicial effect on
Complainant, result in a delay in justice, and undermine the integrity of the system, the Agency’s
rushed investigation produced a shoddy, incomplete ROI, which compounded such harm.
Therefore, w e agree with AJ -2 that a sanction was warranted and consider the appropriate
sanction under the circumstances. AJ-2 ord ered training for the officials responsible for the
Agency not having enough investigators to timely complete EEO investigations and, because

Discrimination Based on Disability, Age, and/or Reprisal
AJ-2 issued a summary judgment decision. The Commission's regulations allow an AJ to grant
summary judgment when he or she finds that there is no genuine issue of mater ial fact. 29
C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). An issue of fact is “genuine” if the evidence is such that a reasonable fact
finder could find in favor of the non -moving party. Celotex v. Cat rett, 477 U.S. 317, 322-23
(1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A fact is “material” if
it has the potential to affect the outcome of the case. We fi nd that the record is sufficiently
developed for summary disposition and that there are no genuine issues of material fact that
require a hearing.

To prevail in a disparate treatment claim, Complainant must satisfy th e three-part evidentiary
scheme fashioned by the Supreme Court in McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792
(1973). He must generally establish a prima facie case by demonstrating that he was subjected to
an adverse employment action under circumstances that would support an inference of
discrimination. Furnco Constr. Co. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567, 576 (1978). Proof of a prima facie
case will vary depending on the facts of the particular case. Mc Donnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at
802 n. 13. The burden then shifts to the A gency to artic ulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory
reason for its actions. Tex. Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). To
ultimately prevail, Complainant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the
Agency’s explanation is a pretext for discrimination. Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products,
Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000 ); St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502, 519 (1993); Burdine,
450 U.S. at 256; Holley, supra; Pavelka v. Dep’t of the Navy, EEOC Request No. 05950351
(Dec. 14, 1995).

Upon review, we agree with AJ -2 that Complainant fa iled to establish a prima fa cie case of
discrimination based on age and/or disability. Complainant offered nothing more than vague
speculation that he was subjected to discrimination based on disability. Moreover, because
Complainant s tated that his only limitations were that he could not run, crawl, or lif t heavy
objects more than 100 pounds, he has not established that he is an individual with a disability for
the purposes of the Rehabilitation Act. Complainant’s Interrogatory at 3.

Further review of the record establishes that Complainant is alleging that the Agency’s process

sensitive information. Rather, Complainant contends that the DRA singled him out, noting that

Moreover, asserts Complainant, while downgrading his clearance, the DRA recommended Top

Complainant has established a prima facie case of reprisal regarding the downgrade of his
security clearance.

Having determined that Compl ainant established a prima facie case of reprisal for claims (4)
through (8), we consider whether the Agency satisfied its burden of production. Although the
Agency's burden of production is not onerous , it must pro vide a specific, clear, legitimate, and
individualized explanation that provides an opportunity for Complainant to satisfy his ultimate
burden of proof of pretext. Lorenzo v. Dep’t of Def ., EEOC Reques t No. 05950931 (Nov. 6,
1997). We find that, without relying on the depositions and other evidence produced for the first
time during discovery, the Agency cannot meet its burden of providing le gitimate,
nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions.

S1’s unsigned investigative affidavit and the limited docum entary evidence in the investigative
record do not satisfy the Agency’s burden to provide legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for
accusing Complainant of missing the deadline as alleged in claim (4), fo r locking Complainant

claims (6) and (7). Regarding claim (8 ), although the investigative record contains a swor n
affidavit from the Chief of the Office of Security for Region IV and some documentary evidence,
the Agency has not identified a specific, clear , legitimate, and individualized explanation for
downgrading the security clearance for Complainant ’s position. We therefore find that
Complainant has established that he was subjected to discrimination based on reprisal as alleged
in claims (4) through (8) and remand the matter for further processing.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), the Agency’s decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.405(a). See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part
1614, at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review
“requires that the Commission examine the rec ord without regard to the factual and legal
determinations of the previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents,
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the
parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and
its interpretation of the law”).

The Commission’s regulations confer upon its AJs very broad responsibility for adjudicating an
EEO complaint once a complainant’s hearing request has been grante d, and that responsibility
gives the AJs wide latitude in directing the terms, conduct, or course of EEO administrative
hearings. Chere S. v. Gen. Serv. Admin., EEOC Appeal No. 0720180012 (Nov. 30, 2018). The
AJ’s discretionary authority includes the power to impose sanctions upon a party that fails to
comply with the AJ’s orders. Id. When the a party fails without good cause shown to respond
fully and in timely fashion to an order of an administrative judge, or requests for the
investigative file, for documents, records, comparative data, statistics, affidavits, or the
attendance of witness(es), the administrative judge shall, in appropriate circumstances: (i) Draw
an adverse inference that the requested information, or the testimony of the requested witnes s,
would have reflected unfavorably on the party refusing to provide the requested information; (ii)
Consider the matters to which the requested information or testimony pertains to be established
in favor of the opposing party; (iii) Exclude other evidenc e offered by the party failing to
produce the requested information or witness; (iv) Issue a decision fully or partially in favor of
the opposing party; or (v) Take such other actions as appropriate. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(f)(3).

Sanctions serve a dual purpose. On the one hand, they aim to deter the underlying conduct of the
non-complying party and to prevent similar misconduct in the future. Barbour v. U.S. Postal
Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 07A30133 (June 16, 2005). On the other hand, they are corrective and
provide equitable remedies to the opposing party. Given these dual purposes, sanctions must be
tailored to each situation by applying the least severe sanction necessary to respond to a party’s
failure to show good cause for its actions and to equitably reme dy the opposing party. Royal v.
Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Request No. 0520080052 (Sept. 25, 2009). Factors pertinent to
“tailoring” a sanction, or determining whether a sanction is even warranted, include: (1) the
extent and nature of the non- compliance, including the justification presented by the non-
complying party; (2) the prejudicial effect of the non- compliance on the opposing party; (3) the
consequences resulting from the delay in justice, if any; (4) the number of times the party has
engaged in such conduct; and (5) the effect on the integrity of the EEO process as a whole. Id.

2021000960

6
The AJ found that the dismissal of Complainant’s hearing request was the appropriate sanction;
however, we have consistently held in our more recent decisions that the dismissal of a hearing
request as a sanction is only appropriate in extreme circumstances. One such circumstance is
when the complainant engages in contumacious conduct, not merely negligence. See Wilma B.
v. Dept. of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 2020003672 (Dec. 2, 2021); Cassey B. v. Dept.
of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 2019004838 (Sept. 24, 2020), request for reconsideration
denied, EEOC Request No. 2021000172 (June 9, 2021); Cecile T. v. Dept . of the Treasury ,
EEOC Appeal No. 2019002373 (Sept. 22, 2020); Carolyn M. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal
No. 2019004843 (Mar. 10, 2020). Examples of contumacious conduct warranting dismissal of
hearing requests include: Charlie K. v. Dep’t of Veteran Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 2019002293
(Sept. 22, 2020) (failure to provide investigative affidavit during agency investigation and failure
to provide answers to interrogatories during discovery despite being granted multiple extensions
in both phases of the proceedings, as well as failure to appear at pre -hearing conference); and
Cleo S. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 0120181406 (Feb. 28, 2020) (failure to
participate in email communications being sought by the agency and to produce documentation
ordered by AJ in a manner demonstrating disregard for the administrative process and
unwillingness to comply with AJ’s orders despite warning of consequences).

These recent cases demonstrate that there must be a showing that a complainant either willfully
disobeyed the AJ’s orders or unjustifiably failed to respond to those orders to justify dismissal of
the hearing request as a sanction. When a lesser sanction would normally suffice to deter the
conduct and to equitably remedy the opposing party, an AJ may be abusing his discretion by
dismissing the complaint. See Georgianne B. v. Dept. of Agric., EEOC Appeal Nos. 0120181591
& 0120181592 (Feb. 27, 2020) (dismissal of hearing request rejected on appeal where AJ
dismissed hearing request outright rather than grant a gency’s motion to compel discovery or

failed to respond to a discovery request despite the fact that the parties and the AJ remained in
continuous email correspondence in an effort to litigate the case); Drucilla Y. v. Dep’t of the
Treasury, EEOC Appeal No. 0120182728 (Feb. 27, 2020) (dismissal of hearing request rejected
on appeal where complainant made earnest but unsuccessful effort to comply with an onerous
acknowledgement and scheduling order), request for reconsideration denied, EEOC Request No.
2020002964 (December 29, 2020).

With the foregoing considerations in mind, we find no indication that Complainant engaged in
the kind of willful or obstinate refusal to comply with the AJ’s orders that typifies contumacious
conduct. On the contrary, there appears to be a genuine dispute between the parties as to whether
Complainant sufficiently complied with the Agency’s discovery requests. Moreover, we note the
more than four-year passage of time between Complainant’s May 24, 2016, submission, and the
AJ’s September 30, 2020, dismissal of her hearing request. During this period, we believe the AJ
could not only have allowed Complainant further opportunity to cure any deficiencies by
providing specific guidance, or crafted a less severe sanction that was specifically tailored to
address a situation where an employee ’s responses to an agency’s discovery request s are not
“full and sufficient.”

In the absence of a showing of either willfully disobedience or an unjustifiable failure to respond,
we cannot find that the integrity of the process has been so compromised as to warrant the severe
sanction of a hearing request dismissal. As such, we conclude that the circumstances in this case
do not justify the particular sanction imposed by the AJ.

DECISION

Complainant filed an appeal, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s October
21, 2020, final decision concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging
employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII),

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Carrier at the
Harlingen Post Office in Harlingen, Texas. Complainant filed a complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against her based on r ace ( White), sex ( female), age ( over 40), and
retaliation (prior EEO a ctivity) in that beginning April 19, 2013, and continuing, she has been
called names, bullied, threatened and intimidated with discharge and/or discipline, including, but
not limited to when:

and provoked during route inspection;

3. In September 2013, she was forced to take her vacation on Leave Without
Pay (LWOP);

4. In approximately the end of April or first of May 2013, she was denied a

5. On unspecified dates, she was denied assistance in fixing problems with

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), the Agency’s decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.405(a). See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part
1614, at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review
“requires that the Commission examine the rec ord without regard to the factual and legal
determinations of the previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents,
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the
parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and
its interpretation of the law”).

The Commission’s regulations confer upon its AJs very broad responsibility for adjudicating an
EEO complaint once a complainant’s hearing request has been grante d, and that responsibility
gives the AJs wide latitude in directing the terms, conduct, or course of EEO administrative
hearings. Chere S. v. Gen. Serv. Admin., EEOC Appeal No. 0720180012 (Nov. 30, 2018). The
AJ’s discretionary authority includes the power to impose sanctions upon a party that fails to
comply with the AJ’s orders. Id. When the a party fails without good cause shown to respond
fully and in timely fashion to an order of an administrative judge, or requests for the
investigative file, for documents, records, comparative data, statistics, affidavits, or the
attendance of witness(es), the administrative judge shall, in appropriate circumstances: (i) Draw
an adverse inference that the requested information, or the testimony of the requested witnes s,
would have reflected unfavorably on the party refusing to provide the requested information; (ii)
Consider the matters to which the requested information or testimony pertains to be established
in favor of the opposing party; (iii) Exclude other evidenc e offered by the party failing to
produce the requested information or witness; (iv) Issue a decision fully or partially in favor of
the opposing party; or (v) Take such other actions as appropriate. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(f)(3).

Sanctions serve a dual purpose. On the one hand, they aim to deter the underlying conduct of the
non-complying party and to prevent similar misconduct in the future. Barbour v. U.S. Postal
Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 07A30133 (June 16, 2005). On the other hand, they are corrective and
provide equitable remedies to the opposing party. Given these dual purposes, sanctions must be
tailored to each situation by applying the least severe sanction necessary to respond to a party’s
failure to show good cause for its actions and to equitably reme dy the opposing party. Royal v.
Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Request No. 0520080052 (Sept. 25, 2009). Factors pertinent to
“tailoring” a sanction, or determining whether a sanction is even warranted, include: (1) the
extent and nature of the non- compliance, including the justification presented by the non-
complying party; (2) the prejudicial effect of the non- compliance on the opposing party; (3) the
consequences resulting from the delay in justice, if any; (4) the number of times the party has
engaged in such conduct; and (5) the effect on the integrity of the EEO process as a whole. Id.

The AJ found that the dismissal of Complainant’s hearing request was the appropriate sanction;
however, we have consistently held in our more recent decisions that the dismissal of a hearing
request as a sanction is only appropriate in extreme circumstances. One such circumstance is
when the complainant engages in contumacious conduct, not merely negligence. See Wilma B.
v. Dept. of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 2020003672 (Dec. 2, 2021); Cassey B. v. Dept.
of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 2019004838 (Sept. 24, 2020), request for reconsideration
denied, EEOC Request No. 2021000172 (June 9, 2021); Cecile T. v. Dept . of the Treasury ,
EEOC Appeal No. 2019002373 (Sept. 22, 2020); Carolyn M. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal
No. 2019004843 (Mar. 10, 2020). Examples of contumacious conduct warranting dismissal of
hearing requests include: Charlie K. v. Dep’t of Veteran Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 2019002293
(Sept. 22, 2020) (failure to provide investigative affidavit during agency investigation and failure
to provide answers to interrogatories during discovery despite being granted multiple extensions
in both phases of the proceedings, as well as failure to appear at pre -hearing conference); and
Cleo S. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 0120181406 (Feb. 28, 2020) (failure to
participate in email communications being sought by the agency and to produce documentation
ordered by AJ in a manner demonstrating disregard for the administrative process and
unwillingness to comply with AJ’s orders despite warning of consequences).

These recent cases demonstrate that there must be a showing that a complainant either willfully
disobeyed the AJ’s orders or unjustifiably failed to respond to those orders to justify dismissal of
the hearing request as a sanction. When a lesser sanction would normally suffice to deter the
conduct and to equitably remedy the opposing party, an AJ may be abusing his discretion by
dismissing the complaint. See Georgianne B. v. Dept. of Agric., EEOC Appeal Nos. 0120181591
& 0120181592 (Feb. 27, 2020) (dismissal of hearing request rejected on appeal where AJ
dismissed hearing request outright rather than grant a gency’s motion to compel discovery or
limiting complainant’s discovery when complainant failed to appear at the initial conference and
failed to respond to a discovery request despite the fact that the parties and the AJ remained in
continuous email correspondence in an effort to litigate the case); Drucilla Y. v. Dep’t of the
Treasury, EEOC Appeal No. 0120182728 (Feb. 27, 2020) (dismissal of hearing request rejected
on appeal where complainant made earnest but unsuccessful effort to comply with an onerous
acknowledgement and scheduling order), request for reconsideration denied, EEOC Request No.
2020002964 (December 29, 2020).

With the foregoing considerations in mind, we find no indication that Complainant engaged in
the kind of willful or obstinate refusal to comply with the AJ’s orders that typifies contumacious
conduct. On the contrary, there appears to be a genuine dispute between the parties as to whether
Complainant sufficiently complied with the Agency’s discovery requests. Moreover, we note the
more than four-year passage of time between Complainant’s May 24, 2016, submission, and the
AJ’s September 30, 2020, dismissal of her hearing request. During this period, we believe the AJ
could not only have allowed Complainant further opportunity to cure any deficiencies by
providing specific guidance, or crafted a less severe sanction that was specifically tailored to
address a situation where an employee ’s responses to an agency’s discovery request s are not
“full and sufficient.”

2021000960

7
In the absence of a showing of either willfully disobedience or an unjustifiable failure to respond,
we cannot find that the integrity of the process has been so compromised as to warrant the severe
sanction of a hearing request dismissal. As such, we conclude that the circumstances in this case
do not justify the particular sanction imposed by the AJ.

Agency for further action in accordance with this decision and the Order herein.

DECISION

On November 30, 2020, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
October 20, 2020, final order concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(Title VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. For the following reasons, the Commission
AFFIRMS the Agency’s final order.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Housekeeping Aide
at the Agency’s John D. Dingell Medical Center in Detroit, Michigan.

On April 29, 2014, August 16, 2014, and September 10, 2014, Complainant filed three EEO
complaints alleging that the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to a hostile

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2021001819

2
work environment on the basis of reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the
Civil Rights Act of 1964 when, among other incidents, he was issued a 14 -day suspension
effective June 22, 2014 through July 5, 2014; on February 14, 2014, he was notified of his non-
selection for the position of Laborer, WG -3502; on June 30, 2014, an Agency police officer
informed Complainant that he could not be on Agency prope rty unless he had an appointment,
and ultimately, he was removed from federal service effective January 25, 2015.
2 See Report of
Investigation for Agency No. 200J-0553-2014-102317 (ROI 1) at 73-74; Report of Investigation
for Agency Nos. 200J -0553-2014-103955 and 200J -0553-2014-104305 (ROI 2) Vol. 1 at 175-
77. Complainant’s removal letter stated that he was to be removed from service based on a
series of incidents supporting two charges: (1) violent, intimidating, and disruptive behavior and
(2) creating a hostile work environment. See Agency’s Brief on Appeal Ex. 4, [Complainant] v.
Dep’t of Vet. Aff., MSPB Docket No. CH -0752-15-0286-I-1 (April 13, 2016) (MSPB Decision
1).

At the conclusion of the investigations , the Agency provided Complainant with copies of the
report of investigation and notices of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing
on the matters and his three EEO complaints were consolidated before the AJ.

At a pre- hearing conference, the AJ agreed with the parties that the hearing should be held in
abeyance pending the MSPB’s decision on Complainant’s challenge to his removal. On April
13, 2016, the MSPB issued an Initial Decision affirming Complainant’s removal , finding
Complainant’s argument that his removal was in retaliation for prior protected activity was
without merit. Specifically, the MSPB found that the evidence in the record and the testimony at
the hearing supported the Agency’s determination that Complainant had crea ted a hostile work
environment due to his contentious behavior with his coworkers, including repeated menacing
looks and noises, verbal threats, isolationist behavior, inappropriate language, and physically
intimidating gestures. See MSPB Decision 1 at 18-19; 26-27. The MSPB further concluded that
there was no evidence in the record to indicate a nexus between Complainant’s removal and his
protected activity. See MSPB Decision 1 at 39. The AJ assigned to the case thereafter adopted
the MSPB’s initial decision and issued an Order Entering Judgment in the Agency’s favor on
September 30, 2020. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding
that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

Complainant filed a petition for review of the MSPB’s initial decision to the MSPB Board.
Complainant also filed an appeal before the Commission of the Agency’s final order adopting
the AJ’s finding, which was held in abeyance pending the MSPB’s decision on Complainant’s
appeal.

treatment pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2) for untimely counselor contact because
Complainant did not contact an EEO counselor about the incident until July 2014, five months
after he received notice of his non- selection. See Report of Investigation (Agency Nos. 103955
and 104305) (ROI 2) Vol. 1 at 175-77.

2021001819

3
The MSPB affirmed its initial decision on July 21, 2022. See [Complainant] v. Dep’t of Vet .
Aff., MSPB Docket No. 0752-15-0286-I-1 (July 21, 2022) (MSPB Decision 2). We now address
Complainant’s appeal to the Commission of the Agency’s final order finding no discrimination.

In rendering this appellate decision, we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and factual conclusions,
and the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a) (stating that
a “decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on a de novo review . . .”);
see also Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO
MD-110), at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (Aug. 5, 2015) (providing that an administrative judge’s
determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed
de novo).

At the outset, we note that the record does not indicate that the AJ provi ded notice to the parties
of her intention to issue a decision without a hearing. The AJ’s decision noted that the parties
discussed the case during the pre-hearing conference, but the conference appears to have focused
on Complainant’s pending MSPB appeal. Commission regulations provide that an AJ may issue
a decision without a hearing on his or her own initiative if the AJ determines that some or all of
the facts are not in genuine dispute. Prior to doing so, the AJ must first give notice to the parties
and provide them with an opportunity to respond in writing. The record in this matter does not
show that the AJ gave the parties notice or the opportunity to respond. However, we find that the
record is adequately developed, and Complainant has not shown that there are genuine issue s of
material fact in dispute.
3 Therefore, we find that the AJ ’s action was harmless and does not
warrant a remand for a hearing. See Alejandro B. v. Soc . Sec. Admin., EEOC Appeal No.
2021002690 (Oct. 6, 2021).

We further find, as a preliminary matter, that contrary to Complainant’s argument on appeal, the
AJ did not exhibit any bias during the course of this case. I n order to prevail on a claim of bias
on the part of an AJ, Complainant must show that the AJ ’s bias against h im “so permeated the
process, that it would have been impossible to receive a fair hearing, or that the process was so
tainted by substantial personal bias that [ he] did not recei ve a fair and impartial hearing.” See
Catheryn P. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 2021002386 (Feb. 28, 2022). In this case,
aside from Complainant’s bare assertion, Complainant has not specified any actions taken by the
AJ to indicate bias nor is t here any evidence to support Complainant’s claim. See Bobbitt v.
Dep’t of Def., EEOC Appeal No. 0120081746 (May 20, 2008).

Upon our review of the record, we agree with the AJ that MSPB Decision 1 accurately recounted
the relevant material facts that were also in the record in the instant matter . We further agree
with the AJ that the evidence in the record does not establish that the Agency subjected
Complainant to either disparate treatment or a hostile work environment based on reprisal for
prior protected activity. We find that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of
discrimination.

3 We also note that the MSPB conducted a hearing prior to issuing its Initial Decision.

2021001819

4
There is no evidence in the record that similarly- situated employees who had not engaged in
protected EEO activity were treated differently for similar inappropriate behavior. See Cheney
v. Dep’t of the Air Force, EEOC Appeal No. 0120060647 (Sept. 7, 2007).

Furthermore, we note that the record is replete with evidence that Complainant had a very
contentious relationship with his coworkers due to his constant and repeated insistence that all of
his coworkers and supervisors were in essence conspiring against him by making false
accusations about his behavior. Complainant’s coworkers and supervisors all agreed that
Complainant did not get along with people and did not like to be supervised or directed in any
way and constantly reported that people were harassing him. See, e.g., ROI 1 at 171-72; ROI 2
Vol. 1 at 321, 377, 385- 86, 393, 404, 429, 466, 492. In addition, we take notice of the MSPB ’s
decision specifically noting that Complainant also displayed a combative attitude at the hearing
before the MSPB AJ. See MSPB Initial Decision 1 at 24-25. We agree with the AJ that the is no
evidence in the record to indicate that any of the Agency’s actions were based on retaliation for
Complainant protected activity. The record shows that the Agency investi gated Complainant’s
reports alleging misconduct by his coworkers and supervisors and took the actions that it deemed
to be appropriate. Moreover, t he evidence in the record indicates that Complainant himself
created a hostile work environment for his coworkers due to his frequent and repeated
inappropriate language and conduct. See Zoey G. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No.
2021000938 (Feb. 16, 2022); Cross v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 0120110281 (Aug.
29, 2012).

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order finding that Complainant
did not establish that he was subjected to discrimination as alleged.
