2022002682

3
On April 17, 2020, the Agency dismissed Complainant ’s complaint pursuant 29 C .F.R.
1614.107(a)(7), for failing to provide relevant information for the processing of her complaint .
On May 8, 2020, the Agency rescinded its April 17, 2020, decision.

On February 3, 2020, the Agency issued an Acceptance Letter dismissing claims 1 thro ugh 9 as
both untimely and under res judicata and collateral estoppel principles. Additionally, the Agency
dismissed Complainant’s hostile work environment claim because it determined that claims 10
and 11 were not sufficient to constitute discriminatory harassment. Complainant responded to the
dismissal.

After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before a n EEOC Administrative
Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing.

On February 2, 2022, Complainant’s counsel filed a motion to reinstate dismissed claims,
seeking to reinstate nine claims back into this case. On February 8, 2022, the Agency responded.

On February 11, 2022, the AJ filed their Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment (Notice). The
AJ denied Complainant’s motion to reinstate the dismissed nine claims. The AJ determined that
claims 1 through 9 were untim ely and dismissed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2).
However, the AJ noted that although a hostile work environment claim was not accepted in the
Notice of Acceptance, they considered the claim and that claim 9 was accepted it to the extent it
was background evidence of Complainant ’s hostile work environment claim as it related t o
claims 10 and 11. As a preliminary matter, the AJ noted tha t Complainant had previously
addressed claim 11 in the Negotiated Grievance Procedure and red uced to a Letter of Warning.
However, to the extent Complainant alleged a collateral attack on the grievance proceeding, such
a claim is dismissed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1) and could not be raised before the
Commission. However, the AJ reviewed claim 11 in the conte xt of Complainant’s employment
discrimination claim. The AJ noted that Complainant had failed to make a prima facie case of
discrimination, unlawful retaliation, or harassment. Further, the AJ indicated that the Agency
had provided legiti mate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant has not
shown was pretext for discrimination. Ultimately, the AJ notified the parties that they were
considering issuing a s ummary judgment in favor of the Agency. The AJ allow ed the parties to
file responses to their Notice. Both parties timely responded.

On March 4, 2022, the AJ issued their decision. The AJ acknowledged the parties’ response to
their Notice . U ltimately, based on a review o f the re cord, the AJ determined that summary
judgment for the Age ncy was still appropriate and entered such a finding. Subsequently, the
Agency issued its final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove
discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

2022002682

4
CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

Complainant did not submit an appellate brief.

In response to the appeal, the A gency asserts Complainant failed to meet the burden of proof ,
below or on appeal, with respect to her claim of harassment and discrimination. The Agency
assets that the AJ accurately summarized the facts and appropriately applied the law in entering
summary judgement in its favor . The Agency requests that the Commission affirm its final
decision adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS
As an initial matter, we note that Complainant did not specifically appeal the dismissal of claims
1 through 9. In this regard, “Although the Commission has the right to review all of the issues in
a complaint on appeal, it also has the discretion not to do so and may focus only on the issues
specifically raised on appeal.” Equal Employment Oppor tunity Management Directive for 29
C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD -110), at Chap. 9, § IV.A.3. (Aug. 5, 2015) . Accordingly, the
Commission will not address the dismissals of claims 1-9 herein.
The Commission's regulations allow an AJ to grant summary judgment when he or she finds that
there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). An issue of fact is
“genuine” if the evidence is such that a reasonable fact finder could find in favor of the non-
moving party. Celotex v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322- 23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp. ,
846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A fac t is “material” if it has the pot ential to affect the
outcome of the case. In rendering this appellat e decision, we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and
factual conclusions, and the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo. See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.405(a)(stating that a “decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on
a de novo review…”); see also EEO-MD-110, at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (Aug. 5, 2015) (providing that
an administrative judge ’s determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decis ion
itself, will both be reviewed de novo).

In order to successfully oppose a decision by summary judgment, a c omplainant must identify,
with specific ity, facts in dispute either within the reco rd or by producing further supporting
evidence and must further establish that s uch facts are materi al under applicable law. Such a
dispute would indicate that a hearing is necessary to produce evidence to suppor t a finding t hat
the Agency was motivated by discriminatory animus. Here, however, Complainant has failed to
establish such a di spute. We note that Complainant chose not to participate in the EEO
investigation and failed to provide an affidavit for the Report of Investigation (ROI). ROI at 157;
169.

Here, the record demonstrated a personality conflict between Complainant and the Coworker .
Report of Investigation (ROI) at 184. The conflict led to a verbal altercation which resulted in
both employees being s ent home without pay (claims 9, 10) . ROI at 184; 187. The verbal
altercation also resulted in Complainant receiving a Seven-Day Suspension, and the Coworker
receiving a 14-Day suspension. ROI at 187.

2022002682

5
In these claims, without proof of a demonstrably discriminatory motive, we will not second-
guess the Agenc y's personnel decisions. see Chavez v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No.
0120055246 (Jan. 5. 2007); see also Carson v. Bethlehem Steel Corp., 82 F.3d 157, 159 (7
th Cir.
1982) (noting that “the quest ion is not whether the employer made the best, or e ven a sound,
business decision; it is whether the real reason [was discriminatory]”).

Ultimately, in revie wing these claims, and even construin g any inferences raised by the
undisputed facts in favor of Complai nant, a reasonable fact finder could not find in
Complainant’s favor. We note that despite given the opportunity to do so, Complai nant did not
provide an appellate brief. Therefore, upon careful review of the AJ’s decision and the evidence
of record, as we ll as all documents submitted on appeal , we conclude that th e AJ correctly
determined that the pre ponderance of the evidence did not establ ish that Complainant was
discriminated against by the Agency as alleged.

Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order adopting the AJ’s decision.

DECISION

On April 13, 2022, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
March 16, 2022, final order concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(Title VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. and the Age Discrimination in Employment
Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the follow ing reasons, the
Commission AFFIRMS the Agency’s final order.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Full -Time City
Carrier at the Agency’s Northwest Station in Plano, Texas.

On September 29, 2019, C omplainant contacted an EEO Counselor. On January 8, 2020,
Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to a hostile work
environment and discriminated against her on the bases of race ( Caucasian), sex (female), and
age (58) when:

following her while she is on and off duty;

3. since November 7, 2011, the Agency has been monitoring and harassing
Complainant through electronic devices;

4. in December of 2011, Complainant’s supervisor asked if Complainant was on

On May 8, 2020, the Agency rescinded its April 17, 2020, decision.

On February 3, 2020, the Agency issued an Acceptance Letter dismissing claims 1 thro ugh 9 as
both untimely and under res judicata and collateral estoppel principles. Additionally, the Agency
dismissed Complainant’s hostile work environment claim because it determined that claims 10
and 11 were not sufficient to constitute discriminatory harassment. Complainant responded to the
dismissal.

After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before a n EEOC Administrative
Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing.

On February 2, 2022, Complainant’s counsel filed a motion to reinstate dismissed claims,
seeking to reinstate nine claims back into this case. On February 8, 2022, the Agency responded.

On February 11, 2022, the AJ filed their Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment (Notice). The
AJ denied Complainant’s motion to reinstate the dismissed nine claims. The AJ determined that
claims 1 through 9 were untim ely and dismissed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2).
However, the AJ noted that although a hostile work environment claim was not accepted in the
Notice of Acceptance, they considered the claim and that claim 9 was accepted it to the extent it
was background evidence of Complainant ’s hostile work environment claim as it related t o
claims 10 and 11. As a preliminary matter, the AJ noted tha t Complainant had previously
addressed claim 11 in the Negotiated Grievance Procedure and red uced to a Letter of Warning.
However, to the extent Complainant alleged a collateral attack on the grievance proceeding, such
a claim is dismissed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1) and could not be raised before the
Commission. However, the AJ reviewed claim 11 in the conte xt of Complainant’s employment
discrimination claim. The AJ noted that Complainant had failed to make a prima facie case of
discrimination, unlawful retaliation, or harassment. Further, the AJ indicated that the Agency
had provided legiti mate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant has not
shown was pretext for discrimination. Ultimately, the AJ notified the parties that they were
considering issuing a s ummary judgment in favor of the Agency. The AJ allow ed the parties to

On March 4, 2022, the AJ issued their decision. The AJ acknowledged the parties’ response to
their Notice . U ltimately, based on a review o f the re cord, the AJ determined that summary
judgment for the Age ncy was still appropriate and entered such a finding. Subsequently, the
Agency issued its final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

Complainant did not submit an appellate brief.

In response to the appeal, the A gency asserts Complainant failed to meet the burden of proof ,
below or on appeal, with respect to her claim of harassment and discrimination. The Agency
assets that the AJ accurately summarized the facts and appropriately applied the law in entering
summary judgement in its favor . The Agency requests that the Commission affirm its final
decision adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS
As an initial matter, we note that Complainant did not specifically appeal the dismissal of claims
1 through 9. In this regard, “Although the Commission has the right to review all of the issues in
a complaint on appeal, it also has the discretion not to do so and may focus only on the issues
specifically raised on appeal.” Equal Employment Oppor tunity Management Directive for 29
C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD -110), at Chap. 9, § IV.A.3. (Aug. 5, 2015) . Accordingly, the
Commission will not address the dismissals of claims 1-9 herein.
The Commission's regulations allow an AJ to grant summary judgment when he or she finds that
there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). An issue of fact is
“genuine” if the evidence is such that a reasonable fact finder could find in favor of the non-
moving party. Celotex v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322- 23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp. ,
846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A fac t is “material” if it has the pot ential to affect the
outcome of the case. In rendering this appellat e decision, we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and
factual conclusions, and the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo. See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.405(a)(stating that a “decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on
a de novo review…”); see also EEO-MD-110, at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (Aug. 5, 2015) (providing that
an administrative judge ’s determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decis ion
itself, will both be reviewed de novo).

In order to successfully oppose a decision by summary judgment, a c omplainant must identify,
with specific ity, facts in dispute either within the reco rd or by producing further supporting
evidence and must further establish that s uch facts are materi al under applicable law. Such a
dispute would indicate that a hearing is necessary to produce evidence to suppor t a finding t hat
the Agency was motivated by discriminatory animus. Here, however, Complainant has failed to
establish such a di spute. We note that Complainant chose not to participate in the EEO
investigation and failed to provide an affidavit for the Report of Investigation (ROI). ROI at 157;
169.

Here, the record demonstrated a personality conflict between Complainant and the Coworker .
Report of Investigation (ROI) at 184. The conflict led to a verbal altercation which resulted in
both employees being s ent home without pay (claims 9, 10) . ROI at 184; 187. The verbal
altercation also resulted in Complainant receiving a Seven-Day Suspension, and the Coworker
receiving a 14-Day suspension. ROI at 187.

2022002682

5
In these claims, without proof of a demonstrably discriminatory motive, we will not second-
guess the Agenc y's personnel decisions. see Chavez v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No.
0120055246 (Jan. 5. 2007); see also Carson v. Bethlehem Steel Corp., 82 F.3d 157, 159 (7
th Cir.
1982) (noting that “the quest ion is not whether the employer made the best, or e ven a sound,
business decision; it is whether the real reason [was discriminatory]”).

Ultimately, in revie wing these claims, and even construin g any inferences raised by the
undisputed facts in favor of Complai nant, a reasonable fact finder could not find in
Complainant’s favor. We note that despite given the opportunity to do so, Complai nant did not
provide an appellate brief. Therefore, upon careful review of the AJ’s decision and the evidence
of record, as we ll as all documents submitted on appeal , we conclude that th e AJ correctly
determined that the pre ponderance of the evidence did not establ ish that Complainant was
discriminated against by the Agency as alleged.

Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order adopting the AJ’s decision.

Complainant asserts, that according to her physician, she had been dealing with depression and

 ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

The Commission’s regulations allow an AJ to issue a decision without a hearing upon finding
that there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). E EOC’s d ecision
without a hearing regulation follows the summary judgment procedure from federal court. Fed.

 4 2022004249

R. Civ. P. 56. The U.S. Supreme Court held summary judgment is appropriate where a judge
determines no genuine issue of material fact exists under t he legal and evidentiary standards.
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 255 (1986). In ruling on a summary judgment
motion, the judge is to determine whether there are genuine issues for trial, as opposed to
weighing the evidence. Id. at 249. At the summary judgment stage, the judge must believe the
non-moving party’s evidence and must draw justifiable inferences in the non- moving party’s
favor. Id. at 255. A “genuine issue of fact” is one that a reasonable judge could find in favor for
the non-moving party. Celotex v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322- 23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip.
Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A “material” fact has the potential to affect the
outcome of a case.

To successfully oppose a decision by summary judgment, a compl ainant must identify, with
specificity, facts in dispute either within the record or by producing further supporting evidence
and must further establish that such facts are material under applicable law. Such a dispute would
indicate that a hearing is necessary to produce evidence to support a finding that the agency was
motivated by discriminatory animus. Here, however, Complainant failed to establish such a
dispute. Even construing any inferences raised by the undisputed facts in favor of Complainant, a
reasonable fact-finder could not find for Complainant.

Claim (1)-Denial of a Reasonable Accommodation Claim

To the extent Complainant claims she was denied a reasonable accommodation, under the
Commission’s regulations, an agency is required to ma ke reasonable accommodation to the
known physical and mental limitations of a qualified individual with a disability unless the
Agency can show that accommodation would cause undue hardship. See 29 C.F.R. §§ 1630.2(o)
and (p).

Because reasonable accommodation is always prospective, an employer is not required to excuse
past misconduct even if it is the result of the individual’s disability. See EEOC Enforcement
Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship Under the ADA, EEOC Notice
No. 915.002 (2002) at Question 36. An employer must make a reasonable accommodation to
enable an otherwise qualified employee with a disability to meet such a conduct standard in the
future, barring undue hardship, except where the punishment for the violation is termination. Id.

In the instant matter, we concur with the AJ that the earliest Complainant put the Agency on
notice of her alleged disability and requested accommodation was by a March 15, 2019 letter
from Complainant to her supervisor. AJ Decision at 9. The March 15, 2019 letter set forth: I
“request your accommodation to allow me necessary time to [recover] and to adjust to the side
effects of the medicine due to my mental disability… ”

Claim (2)-Notice of Removal

A claim of disparate treatme nt is examined under the three -part analysis first enunciated in
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For complainant to prevail, he must
first establish a prima facie case of discrimination by p resenting facts that, if unexplained,
reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e., that a prohibited consideration was a
factor in the adverse employment action. See McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco
Construction Corp. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the agency to
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. See Texas Dep’t of Cmty.
Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the agency has met its burden, the
complainant bears the ultimate responsibility to pe rsuade the fact finder by a preponderance of
the evidence that the agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor
Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

This established order of analysis in discrimination cases, in which the first step normally
consists of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases.
Where the agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action
at issue, the factual inquiry can proceed directly to the third step of the McDonnell Douglas
analysis, the ultimate issue of whether complainant has shown by a preponderance of the
evidence that the agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Serv. Bd.
of Governors v. Aikens , 460 U.S. 711, 713- 714 (1983); Hernandez v. Dep’t of Transportation,
EEOC Request No. 05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Dep’t of Health and Human Services,
EEOC Request No. 05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. De p’t of the Navy, EEOC Petition
No. 03900056 (May 31, 1990).

The Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for issuing Complainant a Notice

DECISION

Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or
Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s July 27, 2022 final action
concerning an equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint al leging employm ent
discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII), as amended,
42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Rehabilitation
Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq.

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Mail Processing Clerk in
Oklahoma City, Oklahoma.

On July 22, 2020, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency
discriminated against her on the bases of her race (African American), national origin (African
American), color (Black), sex (female), and disability (depression and anxiety).

when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

The Agency dismissed Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds and Complainant filed
an appeal. In EEOC Appeal No. 2021000398 (Feb. 11, 2021) , we reversed the dismissal and
remanded the matter to the Agency for an investigation.

Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC
Administrative Judge (AJ). The AJ issued an Order for Supplemental EEO Investigation on
March 25, 2022. Therein, the AJ reframed the issues as follows:

Complainant was discriminated against and subjected to a hostile work
environment…when:

1. She was not granted a reasonable accommodation after requesting an
accommodation from [a named management official] on or about
March 15, 2019; and

2. On April 5, 2019, Complainant was issued a Notice of Removal for
Failure to Maintain Regular Attendance, Absent Without Official
Leave (AWOL), and Failure to Comply with Agency Directives.

The AJ ordered a supplemental investigation on the denial of a reasonable accommodation claim.
Upon completion of the supplemental investigation, the Agency filed a Motion for Summary
Judgment on June 7, 2022. On June 20, 2022, Compl ainant filed a response to the Agency’s
Motion.

On July 19, 2022, the AJ granted the Agency’s Motion and issued a finding of no discrimination
without a hearing. Regarding Complainant’s removal under a disparate treatment analysis, the
AJ found that as suming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case of
discrimination, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. The
AJ stated that “the removal notice noted that since her fourteen- day suspension on Februar y 8,
2019, Complainant had eighteen unscheduled absences.” AJ Decision at 4. The AJ further
found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reason for its action was
pretext for discrimination.

The AJ further found that Compla inant failed to estab lish that the Agency denied her a
reasonable accommodation. The AJ reasoned:

Complainant’s attempts to request an accommodation do not save her claim.
Complainant alleged she discussed a possible disability with [named Agency
officials] on December 17, 2018, when she was issued a seven- day suspension
and on February 8, 2019, when she was issued a fourteen- day suspension, and at
her March 1, 2019 investigative interview and each time she was referred to the
EAP. It is undisputed Compl ainant did not contact EAP until February 25, 2019.
Her individual opinion that she might have a disability that was affecting her

 3 2022004249

attendance was not sufficient to establish a disability or to require the Agency to
provide a reasonable accommodation.

…On March 1, 2019, Complainant stated in her investigative interview that she
could not provide an answer why she was late through February 2019 but that she
had an appointment with EAP, which may be able to explain her issues. Again,
this statement, by its elf was not sufficient to establish a disability or request a
reasonable accommodation.

At best, the earliest Complainant put the Agency on notice of an alleged disability
and requested an accommodation was by her March 15, 2019 letter addressed to
[a n amed management official. The letter mentioned side effects from
medication, which Complainant had just begun taking that day, and depression
and anxiety and requested an accommodation to provide necessary time to
recover. Regardless, an agency is not re quired to excuse past misconduct even if
that misconduct resulted from Complainant’s disability. This is because a
reasonable accommodation request is forward-looking, meaning the Complainant
is entitled to an accommodation only from the date the disabili ty is
disclosed…Thus, the March 15, 2019 letter, to the extent it constituted a valid
accommodation request, did not excuse Complainant’s prior absences. AJ
Decision at 8-9.

The Agency issued a final action dated July 27, 2022 implementing the AJ’s decis ion without a
hearing finding no discrimination.

Complainant filed the instant appeal. On appeal, Complainant asserts, as she did in her response
to the Agency’ s Motion, that the Agency’s supplemental investigation was inadequate.
Specifically, Compla inant states that the supplemental report of investigation did not contain
witness statements she submitted regarding her request for reasonable accommodation.
Complainant asserts, that according to her physician, she had been dealing with depression and
anxiety months prior to receiving treatment from the EAP. Moreover, Complainant assert s that
the Agency improperly terminated her when she was still under treatment from the EAP.

In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final action implementi ng the AJ’s decision.
The Agency asserts that Complainant did not contact EAP until February 25, 2019, and that
Complainant’s personal opinion that she might have a disability that was affecting her attendance
was not sufficient to establish a disability or requir e the Agency to provide a reasonable
accommodation.
 ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

The Commission’s regulations allow an AJ to issue a decision without a hearing upon finding
that there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). E EOC’s d ecision
without a hearing regulation follows the summary judgment procedure from federal court. Fed.

 4 2022004249

R. Civ. P. 56. The U.S. Supreme Court held summary judgment is appropriate where a judge
determines no genuine issue of material fact exists under t he legal and evidentiary standards.
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 255 (1986). In ruling on a summary judgment
motion, the judge is to determine whether there are genuine issues for trial, as opposed to
weighing the evidence. Id. at 249. At the summary judgment stage, the judge must believe the
non-moving party’s evidence and must draw justifiable inferences in the non- moving party’s
favor. Id. at 255. A “genuine issue of fact” is one that a reasonable judge could find in favor for
the non-moving party. Celotex v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322- 23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip.
Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A “material” fact has the potential to affect the
outcome of a case.

To successfully oppose a decision by summary judgment, a compl ainant must identify, with
specificity, facts in dispute either within the record or by producing further supporting evidence
and must further establish that such facts are material under applicable law. Such a dispute would
indicate that a hearing is necessary to produce evidence to support a finding that the agency was
motivated by discriminatory animus. Here, however, Complainant failed to establish such a
dispute. Even construing any inferences raised by the undisputed facts in favor of Complainant, a
reasonable fact-finder could not find for Complainant.

Claim (1)-Denial of a Reasonable Accommodation Claim

To the extent Complainant claims she was denied a reasonable accommodation, under the
Commission’s regulations, an agency is required to ma ke reasonable accommodation to the
known physical and mental limitations of a qualified individual with a disability unless the
Agency can show that accommodation would cause undue hardship. See 29 C.F.R. §§ 1630.2(o)
and (p).

Because reasonable accommodation is always prospective, an employer is not required to excuse
past misconduct even if it is the result of the individual’s disability. See EEOC Enforcement
Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship Under the ADA, EEOC Notice
No. 915.002 (2002) at Question 36. An employer must make a reasonable accommodation to
enable an otherwise qualified employee with a disability to meet such a conduct standard in the
future, barring undue hardship, except where the punishment for the violation is termination. Id.

In the instant matter, we concur with the AJ that the earliest Complainant put the Agency on
notice of her alleged disability and requested accommodation was by a March 15, 2019 letter
from Complainant to her supervisor. AJ Decision at 9. The March 15, 2019 letter set forth: I
“request your accommodation to allow me necessary time to [recover] and to adjust to the side
effects of the medicine due to my mental disability… ”

Claim (2)-Notice of Removal

A claim of disparate treatme nt is examined under the three -part analysis first enunciated in
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For complainant to prevail, he must
first establish a prima facie case of discrimination by p resenting facts that, if unexplained,
reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e., that a prohibited consideration was a
factor in the adverse employment action. See McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco
Construction Corp. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the agency to
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. See Texas Dep’t of Cmty.
Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the agency has met its burden, the
complainant bears the ultimate responsibility to pe rsuade the fact finder by a preponderance of
the evidence that the agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor
Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

This established order of analysis in discrimination cases, in which the first step normally
consists of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases.
Where the agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action
at issue, the factual inquiry can proceed directly to the third step of the McDonnell Douglas
analysis, the ultimate issue of whether complainant has shown by a preponderance of the
evidence that the agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Serv. Bd.
of Governors v. Aikens , 460 U.S. 711, 713- 714 (1983); Hernandez v. Dep’t of Transportation,
EEOC Request No. 05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Dep’t of Health and Human Services,
EEOC Request No. 05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. De p’t of the Navy, EEOC Petition
No. 03900056 (May 31, 1990).

 7 2022004249

The Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for issuing Complainant a Notice
of Removal. The record contains an affidavit from Complainant’s supervisor. Orig. ROI at 268.

problems. Specifically, the supervisor stated “[Complainant] began having attenda nce issues,
claiming that her mother was her sitter and couldn’t arrive in time for her to be at work. I gave

she would be [three] or more hours late. When questioned, she stated that he r mom was
stressing her out, I referred her to EAP before she was issued the first [reprimand and] at each
and every turn, I urged her to seek help from EAP.” Orig. ROI at 271.

The record also contains a Notice of Removal dated April 5, 2019 issued to Complainant. The
Notice stated that Complainant’s remo val is due to failure to maintain regular attendance and
failure to comply with Agency directives. Orig. ROI at 331-334. The record further reflects that
Complainant was previously issued a Notice of Suspension for Seven Days dated December 17,
2018 and No tice of Suspension for Fourteen Days dated February 8, 2019 due to attendance
issues. Orig. ROI at 311-314.

Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s a rticulated reasons for her removal were
pretext for discrimination. While Complainant assert ed that she was treated differently than
other employees who were not terminated due to their attendance issues, the AJ correctly found
that these employees had si gnificantly less unscheduled absences than Complainant. AJ
Decision at 7; Orig. ROI at 284-286.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final action implementing the AJ’s decision without a
hearing finding no discrimination.

Reasonable Accommodation (Claim 23)

To establish that she was denied a reasonable accommodation, Complainant must show that: (1)
she is an individual with a disability, as defined by 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(g); (2) he is a “qualified”
individual with a disability pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(m); and (3) the Agenc y failed to
provide her with a reasonable accommodation. See EEOC Enforcement Guidance on
Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the Americans with Disabilities Act
(Enforcement Guidance), EEOC Notice No. 915.002 (Oct. 17, 2002). A qualified person with a
disability is an individual who can perform the essential functions of the position with or without
an accommodation. As further stated below, Complainant is a qualified individual within the
meaning of the Rehabilitation Act.

Complainant testified that she was diagnosed, in her mid- twenties, with Complex PTSD.
Complainant explained that her condition is permanent. Although Complainant explained that
her condition is controlled with medication and therapy, Complainant acknowledged that when

October 2016, when she applied for and took FMLA leave related to her disability.

that some of her reasonable accommodati on requests would be better handled through the
employee relations/labor relations department. Complainant further indicated that after she had
informed the management officials that she had already filed a formal EEO complaint, her
meeting abruptly ended. During a July 9, 2020 meeting, Complainant stated that she was asked
if she wanted to participate in mediation with the AP . However, Complainant informed
management that she was seeking a reasonable accommodation, not mediation. Thereafter,

Disparate Treatment (Claims 15 -16, 21 -22)

A claim of disparate treatment is examined under the three -part analysis first enunciated in
McDonnell Douglas Corporation v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For complainant to prevail, she
must first establish a prima facie of discrimination by presenting facts that, if unexpla ined,
reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e. , that a prohibited consideration was a
factor in the adverse employment action. See McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco
Construction Corp. v. Waters, 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the agency to
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. See Texas Department of
Community Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the agency has met its burden,
the complainant bears the ultimate respo nsibility to persuade the fact finder by a preponderance
of the evidence that the agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor
Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

This established order of analysis in discrimination cases, in which the first step normally
consists of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases.
Where the agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action
at issue, the factual inquiry can proceed directly to the third step of the McDonnell Douglas
analysis, the ultimate issue of whether complainant has shown by a preponderance of the
evidence that the agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Service
Board of Governors v. Aikens, 460 U.S. 711, 713- 714 (1983); Hernandez v. Department of
Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Department of Health
and Human Services, EEOC Request No. 05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. Department
of the Navy, EEOC Petition No. 03900056 (May 31, 1990).

The record reflects that the Agency articulated legitimate, non -discriminatory reasons for its
actions.

subjected to conduct that was either so severe or so pervasive that a “reasonable person” in
Complainant’s position would have found the conduct to be hostile or abusive. Complainant

Henson v. City of Dundee, 682 F.2d 897 (11th Cir. 1982) ; Harris v. Forklift Systems, Inc., 510
U.S. 17, 21 (1993). See also, Enforcement Guidance on Harris v. Forklift Systems Inc., EEOC
Notice No. 915.002 (March 8, 1994).

by the events in claims 15, 16, 21, and 22 are precluded based on our findings above that
Complainant failed to establish that any of the actions taken by the Agency were motivated by
her disability or reprisal for prior protected EEO activ ity. See Oakley v. U.S. Postal Service ,

brief, and no other members of the team were present. However, the new Nurs e Practitioner was
ultimately introduced to the team during the September 18, 2020 palliative care council meeting.

Non-Selections (Claims 24 -36)

Complainant testified that either she was not interviewed for the positions, or she was
interviewed but was not selected for the positions. Complainant further testified that she believed
that she was “blackballed from transferring away from [the AP]” which resulted in the selecting
officials not hiring her for the various positions. Complainant stated that s he believed that the
AP felt that her use of FMLA leave for her disability was a “negative factor.”

The AP testified she was not involved in the selection process for any of the position vacancies
at issue except for the CRNP (Palliative Care) – CBCC-10629953-20-AA position (Claim 33).
The AP stated that she was a member of the selection committee for this position, and the
position was an inpatient position. In contrast, the AP noted that Complainant, at the time, was in
the outpatient clinic. Consequently, the S electee had a relevant background in providing
inpatient services.

2022001374

15
Additionally, the Nurse Manager testified she was not involved in the selection process for any
of the position vacancies at issue except for the CRNP (Neurology) position, vac ancy number:
CBCC-10592285-19-AA (Claim 29). At the time of this vacancy, the Nurse Manager stated that
she worked in Neurology. Consequently, she served on the interview panel. The Nurse Manager
indicated that Complainant met the basic qualifications f or the position, however, the candidate
chosen for the position had the highest interview score.

We note that the record reflects that Complainant was ultimately hired for the position of Nurse
Practitioner (A Service) under vacancy number CBCC-10675048-20-EW (Claim 36).

Assuming these incidents occurred as alleged, Complainant has not presented sufficient credible
evidence demonstrating that considerations of her disability or retaliatory animus motivated
management’s actions towards Complainant. Here , the majority of Complainant’s allegations
against the AP consisted merely of her disagreements with the AP’s managem ent style and
management decisions. The record reflects that Complainant and the AP did not agree with how
to treat patients and they both complained about each other. The record further reflects that
management informed Complainant of her work deficiencies and much of the information that
Complainant asserted that was withheld from her , was indeed made available during the
palliative council meetings which Complainant was a member. Furthermore, there is insufficient
documentation in the record to suppor t that Complainant was blackballed from transferring to
another position. The record reflects that Complainant applied to several positions, the majority
of which had no involvement by the responsible management officials she identified as
inhibiting her selection, and ultimately, Complainant was reassigned to her preferred position.
The substance of many of these claims involve typical di sputes between an employee and
management. However, we emphasize that EEO laws are not a civility code. Rather, they forbid
“only behavior so objectively offensive as to alter the conditions of the victim’s employment.”
Oncale, 523 U.S. 75, 81 (1998). Aside from Complainant’s bare assertions there is simply no
evidence that the disputed actions were motivated in any way by Complainant’s race, color, sex,
or reprisal for prior protected EEO activity and, therefore, Complainant’s claim of discriminatory
harassment is precluded. See Oakley v. U.S. Postal Servic e, EEOC Appeal No. 019982923
(Sept. 21, 2000).

CONCLUSION

We AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision because the preponderance of the evidence of record
does not establish that discrimination, unlawful r etaliation, or violation of the Rehabilitation Act
occurred.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Reasonable Accommodation (Claim 23)

To establish that she was denied a reasonable accommodation, Complainant must show that: (1)
she is an individual with a disability, as defined by 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(g); (2) he is a “qualified”
individual with a disability pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(m); and (3) the Agenc y failed to
provide her with a reasonable accommodation. See EEOC Enforcement Guidance on
Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the Americans with Disabilities Act
(Enforcement Guidance), EEOC Notice No. 915.002 (Oct. 17, 2002). A qualified person with a
disability is an individual who can perform the essential functions of the position with or without
an accommodation. As further stated below, Complainant is a qualified individual within the
meaning of the Rehabilitation Act.

Complainant testified that she was diagnosed, in her mid- twenties, with Complex PTSD.
Complainant explained that her condition is permanent. Although Complainant explained that
her condition is controlled with medication and therapy, Complainant acknowledged that when
her condition is exacerbated or triggered, she is unable to care for herself , interact with others, or
work. Specifically, Complainant asserted that she was unable to perform her position duties
when she was subjected to the AP’s “abusive treatment” causing her to work in pain and distress.

Complainant explained that the AP and the Nurse Ma nager were aware of her disability since
October 2016, when she applied for and took FMLA leave related to her disability.

Complainant further testified that during a June 24, 2020 meeting, management informed her
that some of her reasonable accommodati on requests would be better handled through the
employee relations/labor relations department. Complainant further indicated that after she had
informed the management officials that she had already filed a formal EEO complaint, her
meeting abruptly ended. During a July 9, 2020 meeting, Complainant stated that she was asked
if she wanted to participate in mediation with the AP . However, Complainant informed
management that she was seeking a reasonable accommodation, not mediation. Thereafter,
Complainant stated that she was notified on August 2, 2020, three months after she had initially

Complainant asserted that the Agency failed to provide justification for denying her reasonable

On May 7, 2020, Complainant submitted a reasonable accommodation for reassignment or

Disparate Treatment (Claims 15 -16, 21 -22)

A claim of disparate treatment is examined under the three -part analysis first enunciated in
McDonnell Douglas Corporation v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For complainant to prevail, she
must first establish a prima facie of discrimination by presenting facts that, if unexpla ined,
reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e. , that a prohibited consideration was a
factor in the adverse employment action. See McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco
Construction Corp. v. Waters, 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the agency to
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. See Texas Department of
Community Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the agency has met its burden,
the complainant bears the ultimate respo nsibility to persuade the fact finder by a preponderance
of the evidence that the agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor
Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

This established order of analysis in discrimination cases, in which the first step normally
consists of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases.
Where the agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action
at issue, the factual inquiry can proceed directly to the third step of the McDonnell Douglas
analysis, the ultimate issue of whether complainant has shown by a preponderance of the
evidence that the agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Service
Board of Governors v. Aikens, 460 U.S. 711, 713- 714 (1983); Hernandez v. Department of
Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Department of Health
and Human Services, EEOC Request No. 05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. Department
of the Navy, EEOC Petition No. 03900056 (May 31, 1990).

The record reflects that the Agency articulated legitimate, non -discriminatory reasons for its
actions.

The AP denied any involvement in the selection process, however, the Nurse Manager indicated

After careful consideration of the record, we conclude that neither during the investigation, nor
on appeal, has Complainant proven, by a preponderance of the evidence, that these proffered
reasons resulted from disparate treatment based on her disability and reprisal for pr ior protected
EEO activity.

Harassment/Hostile Work Environment (Claims 1 – 14, 17 – 20, 24 – 36)

To prove her claim of hostile environment harassment, Complainant mus t establish that he was
subjected to conduct that was either so severe or so pervasive that a “reasonable person” in
Complainant’s position would have found the conduct to be hostile or abusive. Complainant
must also prove that the conduct was taken because of a protected basis – in this case, her
disability or reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. Only if Complainant establishes both of
those elements – hostility and motive – will the question of Agency liability present itself. See
Henson v. City of Dundee, 682 F.2d 897 (11th Cir. 1982) ; Harris v. Forklift Systems, Inc., 510
U.S. 17, 21 (1993). See also, Enforcement Guidance on Harris v. Forklift Systems Inc., EEOC
Notice No. 915.002 (March 8, 1994).

As an initial matter, Complainant’s additional claim of discriminatory harassme nt as evidenced
by the events in claims 15, 16, 21, and 22 are precluded based on our findings above that
Complainant failed to establish that any of the actions taken by the Agency were motivated by
her disability or reprisal for prior protected EEO activ ity. See Oakley v. U.S. Postal Service ,
EEOC Appeal No. 019982923 (Sept. 21, 2000).

Our review of the record supports that Complainant was not subjected to a hostile work
environment as alleged.

Denied Opportunity to LST Conference (Claim 1)

Complainant explained that the AP denied her request to attend this conference because the AP
had determined that Complainant already knew the information presented at the conference even
though Complainant asserted that she did not know this information.

the team. However, Complainant questioned why the Palliative Care Service Program Manager
declined to provide Complainant an opportunity to meet him.

The AP acknowledged that she and the Palliative Care Service Program Manager met with the
new Nurse Practitioner. The AP clarified that due to the Covid- 19 pandemic, the meeting was
brief, and no other members of the team were present. However, the new Nurs e Practitioner was
ultimately introduced to the team during the September 18, 2020 palliative care council meeting.

Non-Selections (Claims 24 -36)

Complainant testified that either she was not interviewed for the positions, or she was
interviewed but was not selected for the positions. Complainant further testified that she believed
that she was “blackballed from transferring away from [the AP]” which resulted in the selecting
officials not hiring her for the various positions. Complainant stated that s he believed that the
AP felt that her use of FMLA leave for her disability was a “negative factor.”

The AP testified she was not involved in the selection process for any of the position vacancies
at issue except for the CRNP (Palliative Care) – CBCC-10629953-20-AA position (Claim 33).
The AP stated that she was a member of the selection committee for this position, and the
position was an inpatient position. In contrast, the AP noted that Complainant, at the time, was in
the outpatient clinic. Consequently, the S electee had a relevant background in providing
inpatient services.

2022001374

15
Additionally, the Nurse Manager testified she was not involved in the selection process for any
of the position vacancies at issue except for the CRNP (Neurology) position, vac ancy number:
CBCC-10592285-19-AA (Claim 29). At the time of this vacancy, the Nurse Manager stated that
she worked in Neurology. Consequently, she served on the interview panel. The Nurse Manager
indicated that Complainant met the basic qualifications f or the position, however, the candidate
chosen for the position had the highest interview score.

We note that the record reflects that Complainant was ultimately hired for the position of Nurse
Practitioner (A Service) under vacancy number CBCC-10675048-20-EW (Claim 36).

Assuming these incidents occurred as alleged, Complainant has not presented sufficient credible
evidence demonstrating that considerations of her disability or retaliatory animus motivated
management’s actions towards Complainant. Here , the majority of Complainant’s allegations
against the AP consisted merely of her disagreements with the AP’s managem ent style and
management decisions. The record reflects that Complainant and the AP did not agree with how
to treat patients and they both complained about each other. The record further reflects that
management informed Complainant of her work deficiencies and much of the information that
Complainant asserted that was withheld from her , was indeed made available during the
palliative council meetings which Complainant was a member. Furthermore, there is insufficient
documentation in the record to suppor t that Complainant was blackballed from transferring to
another position. The record reflects that Complainant applied to several positions, the majority
of which had no involvement by the responsible management officials she identified as
inhibiting her selection, and ultimately, Complainant was reassigned to her preferred position.
The substance of many of these claims involve typical di sputes between an employee and
management. However, we emphasize that EEO laws are not a civility code. Rather, they forbid
“only behavior so objectively offensive as to alter the conditions of the victim’s employment.”
Oncale, 523 U.S. 75, 81 (1998). Aside from Complainant’s bare assertions there is simply no
evidence that the disputed actions were motivated in any way by Complainant’s race, color, sex,
or reprisal for prior protected EEO activity and, therefore, Complainant’s claim of discriminatory
harassment is precluded. See Oakley v. U.S. Postal Servic e, EEOC Appeal No. 019982923
(Sept. 21, 2000).

CONCLUSION

We AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision because the preponderance of the evidence of record
does not establish that discrimination, unlawful r etaliation, or violation of the Rehabilitation Act
occurred.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Claim 1

In Claim 1, Complainant alleged that from 2016 through 2020, management refused to talk to
Complainant, damaged his vehicle, and undermined his authority.

During the period of 2016 through 2020, Complainant worked with four peer -J-Band SFAMs.
He asserted two of his SFAM co -workers (hereafter “CW-1” and “CW-2”) subjected
Complainant to a discrimin atory hostile work environment. The Assistant Federal Security for
Law Enforcement, also Complainant’s supervisor (“S1”) , stated that Complainant, CW -1 and
CW-2 disliked and antagonized one another, and the mutual animosity predated S1’s tenur e at
the Charlotte Field Office.

Complainant stated CW-1 subjected him to harassment w hen she allegedly actively avoided
interacting with him, which CW -1 denied. The record shows that CW -2 stated he and
Complainant disliked each other and that Complainant refused to speak with him and “isolated”
himself from other Charlotte Field Office supervisors. S1 stated that Complainant never made
him aware of any alleged prohibited harassment in relation to CW-1 or CW-2 conduct.

Further, Complainant stated that after getting a monetary award from another EEO complaint, he
purchased a new car. Complainant asserted that that CW-2 damaged his car. Specially, he stated
that in the TSA parking area when CW-2 opened his car. Thereafter, Complainant notified the S1
the alleged conduct and S1 reviewed the parking lot CCTV footage. The record reflects the video
footage confirmed CW-2 parked his vehicle next to Complainant’s car but did not establish that
CW-2 damaged Complainant’s car as alleged.

Complainant claimed that from 2016 to 2020, CW -2 undermined Complainant’s supervisory
authority when he insinuated that Complainant’s supervision would be intolerable, send
Complainant “nasty” emails, and communicated directly with Complainant’s subordinate
employees instead of doing so through Complainant. According to the S1, CW -2 denied the
contact and indicated that Complainant did not report to him.

To prove his harassment claim, Complainant must establish that he was subjected to conduct that
was either so severe or so pervasive that a “reasonable person” in Complainant’s position would
have found the conduct to be hostile or abusive. Complainant must also prove that the conduct
was taken because of a protected basis – in this case, his sex, age, disability and/or prior
engagement in protected activity . Only if Complainant establishes both of those elements –
hostility and motive – will the question of Agency liability present itself. See Henson v. City of
Dundee, 682 F.2d 897 (11th Cir. 1982); Harris v. Forklift Systems, Inc., 510 U.S. 17, 21 (1993).
See also, Enforcement Guidance on Harris v. Forklift Systems Inc. , EEOC Notice No. 915.002
(March 8, 1994).

2022001589

5

discriminatory or retaliatory harassment is precluded by Complainant’s failure to show that any
of the actions taken by Agency officials were motivated by unlawful considerations of his
protected classes. See Oakley v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01982923 (Sept. 21,
2000).

Claims 2 – 5

Federal Air Marshal (SFAM) position in San Francisco, California, under vacancy

witnesses stated they chose the selectee ( “Selectee-1”) (male, age 39) for the subject position
based on his TSA -specific and previous private -sector experience and supervisory
recommendations. During the relevant period, Selectee -1 was a Senior FAM assigned to Law
Enforcement Information Coordination Sector (LE /ICE), where he daily collaborated with
interagency departments at the local, state and federal level. As such, he was considered the best
qualified for the position in question.

Regarding claim 3, in November of 2020, Complainant was not selected for a K -Band SFAM
position under vacancy announcement FAM -20-780437-ERD. Agency management chose
“Selectee-2” (male, approximately same age as Complainant) over Complainant. The selecting
officials stated Sele ctee 2 was chosen due to his varied LE/FAMS and prior law enforcement
experience and was the Assistant Special Agent in Charge at SFO at the time of applicat ion. He
had previously served as Assistant Federal Security Director - Law Enforcement and as Senio r
Level TSA Representative - Executive Board to the Federal Bureau of Investigations, Joint
Terrorism Task Force , where he coordinated numerous high profile dignitary site visits, to
include a site visit by the President of the United States. Selectee 2 also previously served as a
FAM Instructor, Federal Flight Deck 8 Officer Recurrent Training Branch and as a FAM
Instructor at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center and had experience as Police Officer
and Criminal Investigator with the Dallas Police Department Police . In total, Selectee had 29
plus years of law enforcement and training experience. As such, Selectee 2 was considered by
the Agency’s management witnesses to be the best qualified candidate for the position.

not align with her form 50 position;

report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request,
the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision found that,

legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and Complainant did not establish that the
Agency’s reasons were a pretext for discrimination. The decision therefore concluded that
Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

Complainant appealed, contending that the Agency’s reasons should not be believed because
there is no evidence to support them.
3

The Agency did not file a brief in response.

§ 1614.110(b), the Agency's decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.405(a). See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part
1614, at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review
“requires that the Commission examine the record without regard to the factual and legal
determinations of the previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “ review the documents,
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the
parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and
its interpretation of the law”).

2 The Agency initially dismissed claim 2 for untimely counselor contact. Complainant appeal ed
and the Commission reversed the dismissal and remanded the claim for further processing. See
Shana H. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 2021003707 (Sept. 16, 2021). The Agency
also dismissed another claim, alleging that management officials challenged her Workers’
Compensation claim using documentation from an investigation conducted two years prior, for
failure to state a claim as it constituted a collateral attack on another proceeding. See Report of
Investigation (ROI) at 89-92.
3 We note that Complainant initially uploaded her notice of appeal form on April 27, 2022 under
the appeal number associated with her prior appeal. When the error was noticed by the
Commission, Complainant’s appeal was properly docketed under the instant appeal number .
Because Complainant att empted to file her appeal within 30 days of the date the Agency’s
decision was issued, we accept Complainant’s appeal as timely. See Pritchett v. Dep’t of the
Army, EEOC Appeal No. 0120093144 (Sept. 29, 2011).

2022003116

3
Failure to State a Claim

We will first briefly address the Agency’s dismissal of Complainant claim that management
officials challenged her Workers’ Compensation claim using documentation from a two-year-old
investigation. An employee cannot use the EEO complaint process to lodge a collateral attack on
another adjudicatory proceeding. See Wills v. Dep’t of Def., EEOC Request No. 05970596 (July
30, 1998); Kleinman v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05940585 (Sept. 22, 1994). A
claim that can be characterized as a collateral attack, by definition, involves a challenge to
another forum’s proceeding, such as the grievance process, the workers ’ compensation process,
an internal agency investigation, or state or federal liti gation. See Fisher v. Dep’ t of Defense,
EEOC Request No. 05931059 (July 15, 1994). We find that the Agency properly dismissed the
claim pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) as a collateral attack on another adjudicatory
proceeding. See Pamela W. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 2021002142 (June 3, 2021).

relevant legal standards for Complainant to establish that she was subjected to discrimination due
to her race, color, age, or reprisal . We further agree with the Agency’s decision that even
assuming arguendo that Complainant could establish a prima facie case, the Agency articulated
legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and Complainant did not establish that any
of the Agency’s reasons were a pretext for discrimination. Complainant’s Manager stated that
Complainant was assigned to the Level 18 Postmaster position because Complainant’s detail at
the Retail Department had ended and this was the only available position at the time. See Report
of Investigation (ROI) at 241- 43. The Manager explained that Complainant’s title and pay did
not change as a result of the assignment. See ROI at 241-42.

With respect to Claim 2, the Manager stated that Complainant was reassigned from the Mystic
Post Office because there were many complaints about the way Complainant treated other
employees and the employees were going to walk out otherwise. See ROI at 253. Complainant
did not submit any evidence to support her assertions of discriminatory animus but argued only
that the reassignment was unfair because she has never been disciplined. Complainant’s
argument is without merit as the Commission has repeate dly stated that mere assertions or
conjecture that an agency’s explanation is a pretext for intentional discrimination is insufficient

pretext inquiry is not concerned with bad judgment, impeccability, dislike, or a mistake . See
Belia A. v. Dep’t of Homeland Sec’y, EEOC Appeal No. 2021004117 (June 7, 2022).

2022003116

4

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision finding that Complainant
did not establish that she was subjected to discrimination as alleged.

pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a), where the requesting party demonstrates that: (1) the
appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of mate rial fact or law; or (2) the
appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or operations of the

subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of
disability and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when:

1. On December 20, 2019 through March 20, 2020, Supervisor 1 denied Complainant’s
request for advanced leave through the leave donor program and marked her AWOL
(Absent Without Leave).

respond to Complainant’s request for accommodation; denied Complainant information
regarding her leave request/attendance; encouraged/required Complainant to request
leave until the accommodation process was comp leted; created additional barriers to
Complainant’s work environment; discredited Complainant and made her appear
incompetent by using an outdated functional statement to address Complainant’s
accommodation request; failed to engage in the interactive proc ess and falsely reported
Complainant’s medical restrictions; refused to provide Complainant with past functional

the signature block of each email sent to you;” failed to consult with Agency officials
prior to denying Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation; and delayed
reassigning Complainant to a different position.

4. From December 23 through 26, 2019, Supervisor 1 and a Human Resource Specialist
denied Complainant equal access to the reasonable accommodation process, entitlement
information, and Agency forms; failed to take appropriate action to accommodation
requests; failed to acknowledge Complainant’s disability status and documentation on
file; failed to timely process Complainant’s requests; and made additional requests for
medical information that had already been submitted.

Commission) reconsider its decision in Petronila B. v. Department of Veterans Affairs , EEOC
Appeal No. 2021005013 (March 6, 2023). EEOC Regulations provide that the Commission
may, in its discretion, grant a request to reconsider any previous Commission decision issued
pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a), where the requesting party demonstrates that: (1) the
appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of mate rial fact or law; or (2) the
appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or operations of the
agency. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c).

The record reveals that o n March 20, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint , which was
subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of
disability and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when:

1. On December 20, 2019 through March 20, 2020, Supervisor 1 denied Complainant’s
request for advanced leave through the leave donor program and marked her AWOL
(Absent Without Leave).

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2023002746

2
2. On December 20, 2019 through March 20, 2020, Supervisor 1 denied Complainant a
reasonable accommodation, including light duty.

3. From December 23, 2019 through March 20, 2020, Supervisor 1 failed to acknowledge or
respond to Complainant’s request for accommodation; denied Complainant information
regarding her leave request/attendance; encouraged/required Complainant to request
leave until the accommodation process was comp leted; created additional barriers to
Complainant’s work environment; discredited Complainant and made her appear
incompetent by using an outdated functional statement to address Complainant’s
accommodation request; failed to engage in the interactive proc ess and falsely reported
Complainant’s medical restrictions; refused to provide Complainant with past functional
statements; demonstrated offensive behavior when stating, “My phone number is listed in
the signature block of each email sent to you;” failed to consult with Agency officials
prior to denying Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation; and delayed
reassigning Complainant to a different position.

4. From December 23 through 26, 2019, Supervisor 1 and a Human Resource Specialist
denied Complainant equal access to the reasonable accommodation process, entitlement
information, and Agency forms; failed to take appropriate action to accommodation
requests; failed to acknowledge Complainant’s disability status and documentation on
file; failed to timely process Complainant’s requests; and made additional requests for
medical information that had already been submitted.

5. On February 14, 2020, Supervisor 1 placed Complainant in an unapproved leave status
and sent Complainant an AWOL notification.

6. On April 30, 2020, Supervisor 1 denied Complainant access to “fair and equal benefits,”
training, and the reasonable accommodation process.

position.
2

subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s final decision to
the Commission. In our prior decision, we affirmed the Agency’s decision finding no
discrimination. We found Complainant failed to show that the Agency denied her reasonable
accommodation or engaged in any action that constituted a violation of the Rehabilitation Act.

2 The Agency dismissed an allegation regarding a denial of Family and Medical Leave Act
(FMLA) as a collateral attack on another administrative process. The Commission affirmed the
Agency’s dismissal of this claim noting the proper forum to challenge an eligibility
determination for FMLA is through the Department of Labor’s FMLA enforcement procedures.

2023002746

disparate treatment or harassment.

Complainant notes that when the Commission’s prior decision was issued, the Agency had not
provided the Commission the entire rep ort of investigation. In response to Complainant’s
request, the Agency acknowledges the mistake and provides evidence indicating that the missing
documents were due to a system update. Further , the Agency correctly notes that Complainant
did not raise her concern about missing documents in her prior appeal.

In her request for reconsideration Complainant provides no evidence to warrant granting her
request. With regard to her contention that the Commission did not have the full report of
investigation at the time our prior decision was issued, we note th at the Commission has since

DECISION

Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or
Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s April 1, 2023, final
decision concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging employment
discrimination in violation of Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Rehabilitation Act),
as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq. For the following reasons, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final
decision.

BACKGROUND

During the relevant time , Complainant worked as a Program Liaison Specialist at the Agency’s
External Affairs O ffice in Washington, D .C. Complainant was a reservist employee with
temporary/intermittent status. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 290. As a Program Liaison
Specialist, Complainant’s duties included providing onsite American Sign Language (ASL)
support to members of the public during disaster relief operations. Report of Investigation (ROI)
at 260, 262. After Complainant grew concerned about the manner in which the Agency provided
assistive communication services to the public, she raised her concerns with management.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2023002985

2
On January 11, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated
against her in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (opposition to Agency’s failure to provide
adequate assistive communication services to members of the public) under the Rehabilitation Act
when:

1. On October 8, 2021, management removed Complainant’s duties and transferred them
to another employee;
2. On October 9, 2021, management demobilized Complainant;
3. On October 10, 2021, management issued Complainant a negative performance rating;
4. On October 18, 2021, management placed Complainant in an unpaid/unavailable
status; and
5. On March 21, 2022, management terminated Complainant’s contract.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report
of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but
subsequently withdrew her request after the AJ ordered her to show cause as to why her hearing
request should not be dismissed for her failure to submit a preliminary case information report.
Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) , which
concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as
alleged. Complainant then filed the instant appeal challenging the Agency’s finding of no
discrimination.
2

STANDARD OF REVIEW

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b),
the Agency’s decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a).
See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614, at Chapter 9,
§ VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review “requires that the
Commission examine the record without re gard to the factual and legal determinations of the
previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents, statements, and testimony of
record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the parties, and . . . issue its decision
based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and its interpretation of the law”).

2 Complainant also challenges the AJ’s decision to issue a Show Cause Order and argues that she
did not receive the AJ’s orders due to her deployment . However, we decline to address the
propriety of the Show Cause Order because the record clearly shows that Complainant knowingly
and voluntarily withdrew her hearing request.

 2023002985

3
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

A claim of disparate treatment is examined under the three -part analysis first enunciated
in McDonnell Douglas Corporation v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For Complainant to prevail,
she must first establish a prima facie case of discrimination by presenting facts that, if unexplained,
reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e., that a prohibited consideration was a
factor in the adverse employment action. See McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco Constr.
Corp. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the A gency to articulate a
legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for its act ions. See Tex. Dep't of Cmty. Affs . v. Burdine,
450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the Agency has met its burden, the complainant bears the ultimate
responsibility to persuade the fact finder by a preponderance of the evidence that the agency acted
on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

In this case, assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination,
we find that Agency management articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for its actions.
As to claims 1 and 2, External Affairs Officer denied that any of her duties were removed. ROI at
262. Rather, he explained that Complainant was needed to help secure an ASL contract. ROI at
262. Complainant provided field support and helped secure the ASL contract. ROI at 262. Once
the contract was secured, External Affairs Officer explained, the responsibility of managing the
contract was given to a Region 2 employee for continuity, and Complainant’s tasks were
considered completed, and her services were no longer needed. ROI at 262-63. External Affairs
Officer conceded Complainant was demobilized sooner than expected but said that it was because
her job was completed. ROI at 265.
For claim 4, the Agency explained that Complainant was made unavailable for deployment in
October 2021 because the Agency received a complaint regarding Complainant’s conduct while
deployed and it was Agency policy to make individuals unavailable during the pendency of the
internal investigation. ROI at 13 and 89.

Finally, as to claims 3 and 5, the Agency explained that management issued Complainant a
negative performance rating and terminated her contract because Complainant did not consistently
perform all of her duties at the “Achieved Expectations” standards for her position’s core
competencies. ROI at 137. In this case, Complainant’s performance was rated as “unacceptable,”
because she demonstrated weaknesses in the core competencies of communication, teamwork, and
cooperation, as she not only circumvented the chain of command and requested products for public
consumption from headquarters without prior approval from her supervisor, but also incorrectly
told field leadership that Agency ASL interpreters were required at all media events. ROI at 106-
07 and 137. Complainant’s statement to field leadership was found to be inaccurate, as
headquarters later clarified that ASL interpretation for media events hosted by state and local
government were the responsibility of the host government and not the Agency. These events, as
well as the complaint against Complainant, resulted in an unacceptable rating and ultimately led
to her termination for poor performance. ROI at 15 and 106-07.

We ultimately find no persuasive evidence that Complainant’s prior EEO activity played a role in
any of the Agency’ s actions. At all times, the ultimate burden remains with Complainant to

 2023002985

4
demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that the Agency’s reasons were not the real
reasons and that the Agency acted on the basis of discriminatory animu s. Complainant failed to
carry this burden. While Complainant repeatedly attempts on appeal to rationalize her conduct and
argue that the Agency retaliated against her for opposing discrimination against members of the
public, Complainant has not proffered any persuasive evidence from which a reasonable fact finder
could conclude that the Agency’s explanation for its actions was pretext for discrimination.
To the extent that Complainant is alleging that s he was subjected to a hostile work environment,
the Commission finds that under the standards set forth in Harris v. Forklift Systems, Inc. , 510
U.S. 17 (1993), Complainant's claim of hostile work environment must fail. See Enforcement
Guidance on Harris v. Forklift Sys., Inc., EEOC Notice No. 915.002 (Mar. 3, 1994). Complainant's
harassment claim is precluded based on our finding that s he failed to establish that any of the
actions taken by the Agency were motivated by discriminatory or retaliatory animus. See Oakley
v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01932923 (Sept. 21, 2000).

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision.

elects to file a statement or brief in support of the request, that statement or brief must be filed
